Why is the Dominion Government building a bridge at Banff? Is it for the National park?	.
This is a re-vote for repairs to a bridge in the National park.
Has this expenditure been recommended by the Department of the Interior?
Yes.
It looks like a provincial work.
The Dominion Government has to look after the bridges in the national parks.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext:
Hon. gentlemen all know that the Banff National park is owned and administered by the Dominion Government. It is perhaps one of the greatest sources of revenue that we have in that line in the western country. It attracts a lot of tourists, who leave a large amount of money with the railways, and with the residents. Undoubtedly the old bridge over the Bow

river requires repairing, and I think $3,000 is a moderate sum. But in view of the present condition of our finances I think the Government might hold up for a while, until labour is cheaper and the work can be done more economically. $100,000 is a lot of money for a new bridge that is to be built just about 30 or 35 feet west of the present one and I understand the abutments aire already in. Perhaps if we passed this item for repairs, the minister would promise not to go on with the new bridge for a while.

I do not think we should strike out the item for the new bridge at that point because it is absolutely necessary. The bridge now being used is unsafe, and it is the duty of the Government to go ahead with the construction of a new one with the least possible delay. If we struck out this $100,000 item the new bridge could not be completed for two years. We want to get the heaviest part of the work done in the fall and winter when the water is low. There are no abutments there at the present time, so far as II know. Tenders were called for and the tender accepted was in the vicinity of $100,000, but that will not complete the bridge. This new bridge is an absolute necessity for the safety of the people who are using the park.

As stated by the hon. member (Mr. Tweedie) this new bridge is an absolute necessity, and its construction has been strongly urged by the Department of the Interior. Before these Estimates were submitted to Parliament every oare was taken to strike out every item that we could possibly hold over for another year.
Why is the Federal Government building a bridge in the province of Alberta? I understood that the province looked after its own highways.
This bridge is on the private property of the Dominion Government at Banff. It is not a provincial matter at all.

The minister says the bridge is on the private property of the Dominion Government. Can we in view of the state of our finances afford to expend $100,000 on a bridge on private property which we are not using? If there is any use of the park it must be by the people of the province and visitors to that province. There is no revenue coming to this Government from the park, I suppose.

I cannot say as to that. While this park iis 'the private property of the Dominion Governmeht it is open to the public. The Provincial Government has no jurisdiction over the park or its roads and bridges. We could not ask the Provincial Government to assist us in building ja bridge in this park any moire than we could ask them to build a bridge over a stream on, the experimental farm at Ottawa, notwithstanding that many people in the province visit that farm.

I fail to see 'the analogy between the experimental farm at Ottawa and this territory in question. I understand that this park is a beautiful tract of land owned by the Dominion Government, but so far as I know the traffic over the bridge under discussion is altogether local. If the minister can satisfy me that lit its the duty of the Dominion Government to build, a bridge in that place, (that is another matter.

If the hon. member (Mr. McKenzie) would visit the town of Banff he would understand the situation. Banff town is under the jurisdiction of the Dominion Government (having been incorporated vnder an Act passed in 1887); which exercises over it 'the same rights as a municipal council exercise over other towns in the province. The Dominion Government own and operate the sewerage system and the water system; they own all the streets and boulevards; and they receive a revenue from the land, which i& leased for a term of years to the settlers. I do not think there is any question whatever as 'bo the absolute necessity for the .bridge, (which crosses the Bow river.
Air. MoMASTER: What is the population of Banff on both sides tributary to the (bridge?

I do not know, but I
have been in Banff and it & quite a town.
Quite a small town.

It is a considerable .town. There are a good many thousand people there for many months of the year. If ithe hon. member has ever been in Banff he mupt know that the bridge is a neoes-jSity. 'The last time I was there (it was not in good condition. It is not a credit to the ^Dominion Government that the bridge should (be as it is.

Has the minister any
figures regarding the number of tourists who use this bridge.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: We were told last year by some hon. member from the West that there were solemn promises from the Prime Minister, not only once but half a dozen times, that the natural resources of the western provinces were to be handed over to the provinces. This is a natural resource, and I suppose that when it is handed over bridges and every other improvement will go with it. It is not very likely that we shall retain any parks if we pass over the natural resources to the provinces, and if that is to happen in the near future, I do not think it advisable for us to spend large sums of money upon property which may soon pass out of our hands. 'It would be interesting to know whether the income from this place is sufficient to justify us in this expenditure. I for one would be satisfied that any monies derived from that park should be devoted to the upkeep of its bridges and other necessary works, but if it is not sufficient the proposition is altogether different.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The bridges to which the hon. member refers would be new constructions. This is to take care of a construction that already exists. It is true that a new bridge is to be put up, but the traffic and all the other conditions that call for this expenditure have been created by the very fact of the bridge being there. Furthermore, the property is altogether our own property, for which this Government is directly responsible, and we are running a grave risk indeed if we keep there a bridge which is unsafe. The cases are wholly different. As regards a new construction, the statement made by the Minister of Finance, as related by the hon. member, is quite true. As to what the hon. member for North Cajpe Breton (Mr. McKenzie) says, the revenue derived from the parks does not go to the Dominion Treasury; it goes to the people of Canada in many ways. Railway traffic is developed, retail business is increased, and money is brought into the country and spent in many ways. The whole people get the advantage. As regards the handing 'back of these parks, I do not know that even on the return of the resources the provinces would desire the parks handed back. They are naturally a national rather than a provincial asset. They are the recreation grounds of the whole people. Indeed, at the provincial conference the suggestion that the parks should not become provincial property was, if I understand, acquiesced in generally by the provinces themselves.

The minister has only answered part of my question. Regarding the bridge at Campbellton, a

new structure was highly desirable, and the provinces were willing to contribute. But worl; on the wharf at Gascons, where there are 100 fishermen, was held off after the contract was awarded. Evidently the Government made a mistake in that because we have the same amount in the Estimates this year notwithstanding their declaration last year that there was no commercial necessity for the work.

There were works that were not carried out last year on account of financial conditions. We have made a survey of all the works in connection with every item and it is the intention to proceed with these works as soon as the Estimates are passed for the reason that we believe they are of urgent necessity.
How is the town of Banff administered and what is the cost of administration?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The town of Banff is administered by the Parks Branch of the Department of the Interior. Leases are given of the town properties and lots, and conditions are attached looking to the perpetuation of the beauty of the town and park. The town is laid out in the first place by town planners, and generally nothing can be done except under license or permit from the proper authority. A justice is appointed there under authority of the Governor in Council and before that justice cases are tried. I do not know what the arrangement is .between him and the judicial authority. The general lines of administration have not been altered in years, nor has the principle of maintenance and collection of revenue. Attempts have been made to reduce the levies, but we have not yielded except to do for returned soldiers in relation to the parks the same as is done by the provinces in the territory under their jurisidction.

Waghorn's Guide,
which I understand to be a standard work of its kind, gives Ithe population of Banff as 500.
All the year round?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
That is only in winter.
iMr. McMASTER:	I would imagine that
in summer there would be a large tourist traffic but I understand that moslt of the natural features of scenic beauty are on the same side as the hotel and that the bridge is nolt used by tourists to any great extent. That is my recollection of a visit

I paid there in exceedingly good company some five years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman is
mistaken; the bridge is between the station and Ithe hotel. Everybody has to use it.

The hotel, I understand
is owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There is the Canadian Pacific Railway hcftel and there is the Dr. Brett sanitarium. I do not know how many there are.

The minister says we
have to build this bridge to protect life. Any expenditure to protect life is justified but as a nation Ithat is desperately hard up, could hot the present situaltion be met by an expenditure of less than $100,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not think a proper bridge could be erected for less than that sum. I was not anxious Ito spend a large sum and I was responsible for postponing the vote for two years but I thought I could not take the responsibility longer. The character of the. structure was thoroughly canvassed and we endeavoured to reduce the cost. A slightly cheaper bridge could have been built bult it would have been an unwise investment in the opinion of the officials in whom I have confidence and it would have been inappropriate to the character of the surroundings and the purpose of the bridge. It would have been an eyesore rather than an addition to the beauty of the park.

The question raised by the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) concerning the policy of the Government in relation to bridges might well be considered in a broader way and perhaps at some more convenient time some clearer declaration might be made of the policy of the Government. International bridges, I take it for granted, would be a matter of arrangement between the Canadian Government and the Government of the United States. It may be that interprovincial bridges would also be a proper subject for the Dominion, but it is within my knowledge that a few years ago interprovincial bridges were refused aid by the Government, whereas bridges built within a province have been aided largely. I do not say this by way of criticism but difficulties arise as to the class of bridge that properly comes under the supervision of the Dominion Government and if at a convenient moment

the hon. gentleman could endeavour to draw the line a little more clearly it would probably prevent some discussion that would otherwise arise. Difficulties have arisen in the past because when a project for the building of a bridge was advanced somebody would say:	"There is no use
bothering about that; ithe Dominion Government will not do anything; it is a provincial undertaking." If we had some clearly defined line as to the responsibility of the Dominion and of the provinces it would be very helpful.	,

The policy of the Government in the past-, and the same policy ie being pursued to-day, has been to assist i.n the construction of intenprovincial bridges, as for example the bridge between Ottawa and Hull; to build bridges over canals or public [works owned entirely by the Bo-minion; and to aid in the construction of international bridges.

In the case of a bridge being constructed partly for railway and partly for highway purposes-not being international, and not being interprovin-cial-would not the Government aid that construction in some cases?

No, there has been no aid of -that bind. I can recall >a case, however, in 'the province oif Quebec, where, with respect 'to a bridge crossing -one of our own canals, aid was granted under arrangement made with the municipality.
The Victoria bridge 4s an example of such federal assistance.

We have also given aid in the case of -a railway crossing' -a river. I remember that w,as done in the case of the Edmonton and Dunvegan railway, which -crosses some large Stream in 'the West. It was represented to us that the bridge wa-s going -to cost a million dollars and a subsidy was -asked ter. A special amount was voted for assistance in that case.

In the
case of the Victoria -and Gharl-e nagne bridges, highway bridges were -attached to those structures. Dominion -aid was given in both cases.
Under the Railway Act there is a provision iter the Government 'to join with a municipality in constructing a large railway bridge, the municipality paying fits portion of 'the cost.

The hon. member for Bonav-enture has referred to the Victoria bridge. If -my memory serves me correctly that bridge was built toy the Grand Trunk Company 'themselves, and they charge a toll for i-ts use.
The work was heavily subsidized by the Dominion.
The reason ter that may have been that it crosses the St. Lawrence river.

The Charlemagne bridge crosses the Riviere des Prairies and a highway bridge was attached to it, and on that condition it received a Dominion subsidy. The same assistance has -been applied for to aid in building a bridge between Ste. Anne and Vaudreuil for the last twenty years to my knowledge. The hon. gentleman's predecessor in the administration of the Public Works Department (Hon. Mr. Monk) gave a pledge on behalf of the Dominion Government that they would contribute fifty per cent of the cost -of that bridge if the province would pay the difference, and that offer still stands.

I cannot say what the late Mr. Monk promised with reference to a subsidy for that particular bridge. I know the place well and there is great need for a proper connection there. I think it is almost a disgrace to Canada that no bridge has been provided during the last forty v-ears. An automobile or a carriage desiring to cross at that point has to -be ferried on a scow. But that is an entirely provincial matter; I do not see why the Dominion Government should assist in the construction of such a bridge as that. As I already said, we have granted aid for construction of highway bridges in Quetoec, but only where they crossed a Government canal.
The Federal Government has a canal at Ste. Anne, and that was why the late Mr. Monk gave the pledge referred to.

The proper way to give the needed accommodation at the point in question would be to attach a highway bridge to the present railway bridge. As I understand it, the railway company is quite willing to grant the necessary permission, but the authorities-either provincial or municipal-as I understand object to the expense. The expense would not be so awfully great, and I cannot understand why

the provincial authorities have not long ago provided a highway bridge there.

The Provincial Government have promised to subscribe fifty per cent of the cost of a new bridge at the point referred to provided the Dominion Government would do the same. The late Mr. Monk promised that the Federal Government would contribute its -share, not because the proposed bridge was interpro-vineial, but by reason of the fact that it would be a public utility. Under the circumstances, I do not see why the Government should not carry out the undertaking entered into by that gentleman. In the event of the Dominion and provincial authorities contributing toward the cost of a bridge at St. Anne the municipality of Isle Perrot will do its share.
A committee composed of some of the most influential men in the industrial and professional life of Montreal interviewed the Federal Government a few weeks ago to secure a grant towards the construction of this bridge, but they were told: " We have heavy commitments to meet and we must be economical." Well, we are ready to admit that principle of economy, but it should be applied impartially to every part of the country. If the Government is ready to build a bridge at Banff or anywhere else, presumably it is because it is a necessary public work. This bridge that I am asking assistance for is also a necessary public work, and therefore I submit the Government should treat it in the same way as it treats the Banff bridge* they should build it or contribute towards its cost. The Boards of Trade of Toronto and all the towns between Toronto and Montreal have sent resolutions to the Government recommending the construction of this bridge, and its importance and necessity is admitted generally. I do not know why the Government is so parsimonious in this particular case. I would suggest that it grant substantial financial assistance towards the construction of this very important bridge at Ste. Annes and Vaudreuil.

I agree with the hon. member that the Ontario and Quebec municipalities have sent resolutions to the Dominion Government recommending the construction of this bridge. But they are not the only people who send resolutions when they want money expended that they should themselves expend. I cannot see why every time a bridge or some other work that is really a provincial undertaking is required that the Dominion Government should be
[Mr. J. D. Reid.l
called upon to build it. I have no recollection-and the deputy minister confirms me [DOT]-of any case where the Dominion Government have ever built or assisted to build what is really a provincial bridge and for which the Provincial Government alone is responsible. That being the case, if we place in the Estimates an item for this bridge, we are at once faced with further expenditures of the same character, for the provinces are frequently applying for federal assistance on the ground that the works contemplated involve a very large expenditure and the Dominion Government should assist the Provincial Government, and a grant .such as my hon. friend is now asking for would be used as a precedent for further demands on the Federal Treasury. This bridge is entirely a provincial matter.
It is across the canal at Ste. Anne's.

Certainly the Federal Government should assist if this were a low level bridge. But a highway 3 p.m. bridge can be built at Ste.
Anne's without interfering with navigation in any way. The bridge is going to be a high level bridge. The hon. member shakes his head.
No.

Of course, he can use the argument that it is to be a low level bridge, but I know the location well, and the connection required could be obtained at the least possible expenditure by simply putting a roadway between the Canadian Pacific and the Grand Trunk bridges. The hon. member may say that the bridge will be built across the canal to get the necessary item put in the Estimates, but I am sure no engineer would advise the building of such a bridge. I am convinced that the advice would be to take advantage of the two railway bridges and build the highway bridge between them.

We asked the Canadian
Pacific Railway Company and the Grand Trunk Railway Company for permission to construct a bridge betwen the two railway bridges. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company was ready to allow us to do so, but the Grand Trunk Railway Company refused. No doubt such a bridge would be less expensive, but, apart from the refusal of the Grand Trunk Railway Company it *is feared) that a highway between the two railway bridges would be very difficult to

keep open during the winter on account of the snow drifting there. If we go below the railway bridges we must cross the canal, and then the Federal Government should certainly pay. I wish to know if any assistance will be given.

I would not want to agree to build a low level bridge that for all time to come we would have to maintain and operate over the canal. Of course, I am not putting my judgment against that of any engineers who may look over the situation, but my advice would be to build the bridge either between the two railway bridges or on either side of them. If the Canadian Pacific Railway are willing to agree to its bridge being made use of, I will take the matter up with the Grand Trunk Railway Company and see whether they too will agree to the use of their bridge so that the highway may be constructed between the two bridges.

There is another objection to building between the two railway bridges, and that is the great cost of building the approaches, which is a very serious objection. However, if the minister can convince thp Grand Trunk Railway Company of the feasibility of this highway bridge between the two railway bridges, I would like to know if the Government will help in any way towards the cost of construction. The first estimate was $300,000. The minister himself told me that we must add a large sum to that estimate. Supposing the bridge will cost $500,000, and the province of Quebec will contribute $250,000, then the municipalities would have to contribute the balance, if the Federal Government does not assist. But the municipalities are not able to do so. Already they have expended nearly a million dollars on improved highways, and in that way they are setting a good example to the country. The proposed bridge will be used not only for local traffic, but for interprovincial traffic, for this will be the connecting link of the provincial highways between Toronto and Montreal. Therefore it is only reasonable that we should have assistance from the Federal Government.

The Quebec Government should take this matter up with the Ontario Government. This bridge is only a few miles from the main highway of the province, and if any contribution should be given, it certainly should come from the provincial governments and not from the Dominion Government. The hon. member
says that the Quebec Government will contribute one-half the amount.
Yes.
From the information I have I understand that the local municipalities are ready to subscribe the rest.
No, but they will guarantee part of the cost,

The municipalities are willing to do that provided they are allowed to collect tolls in repayment of the portion they contribute. That would settle the trouble. I -would suggest that the several local municipalities form themselves into a corporation to build this connecting link as a toll road and obtain powers under their charter to levy tolls until they have recouped themselves their capital expenditure. There is a heavy tourist traffic in this district and in this way they will be able to carry out their undertaking without seeking assistance from the Dominion Treasury.
Would the same policy apply to the bridge at Banff?

The bridge alt Banff
is our own property, and we canont get any aid from the province of Alberta in connection with it.

The question of building the proposed bridges alt Ste. Anne and Vaudreuil has been a subject of discussion for the paslt fifty years. I remember years and years ago when the late Hon. Mr. Laflamme and the late Mr. Justice Girou-ard, who formerly represented Jacques Cartier, which I now have the honour to represent, were discussing the question of Ithose bridges. At every election contest, if one or the other was elected, he promised that he was certain to have the bridges constructed. The Hon. Mr# Laflamme was elected twice; the Hon. Mr. Girouard was eledted three times, but the bridges have not yet been constructed. I was elected for Jacques Cartier for the first time in 1911, having previously represented Montcalm, and I pledged my word of honour that if I were eledted, the bridges would be built. In that I followed the example of and the declaration given by the late Hon. F. D. Monk, when he represented Jacques Cartier. Every time he was elected from 1896 to 1911, the same promises were made, but no bridge has been built. The same difficulty has always arisen. I agree, perhaps for the first time, with the minister; he would do a great favour and

render great services to my electors if he would do what he has just stated should be done. I discussed the matter with the late Mr. Vallee, chief engineer of Quebec province, and he was of opinion that the two railway bridges now in existence are sufficiently strong to have a passerelle between them. In the present state of the finances of the country, I would suggest to the minister that that should be constructed so as to render a service to the electors of Jacques Cartier, Ste. Anne, Vaudreuil and all the surrounding country. When we are not able to get a full loaf, we are prepared to take half a loaf, and laiter on, when the Liberal party comes into power-and I hope that will not be very long-we shall be able to do something else. But for the present the minister should do what he has just stated, namely, try to help us to get that highway bridge constructed by using the two railway bridges already built. This is not a provincial question, because these two bridges are a matter of interest to the whole Dominion. The minister has built a very large military hospital at Ste. Anne, and my electors and I are very glad that he has done so. Millions were spent there and the expenditure was necessary. This is a Dominion military hospital receiving patients from every part of the Dominion, but how can you reach that military hospital at Ste. Anne when there is no bridge? Millions and millions of dollars were spent at Macdonald College at Ste. Anne, the best institution in the whole Dominion of Canada. The late Sir William Macdonald gave five or six million dollars to that college. In a few days we shall have an international agricultural concours there with representatives from every province, and in my opinion the Government should see that provision is made that Macdonald College, and the military hospital built by the Government, may be reached from every province. When the late Mr. Monk represented Jacques Cartier with so much honour to himself and with so much benefit to the electors of that constituency, he declared publicly in my presence at a large public meeting held in Jacques Cartier-and he was a man who never failed in his word-that the duty of the Federal Government was to do its best to have those two bridges built. I am sure that the minister will see that full justice is done to the electors of Jacques Cartier, not because I represent that constituency, not because I ask for this, but because it is a measure of simple justice to the 
travelling public of the Dominion of Canada.

Those bridges at Ste. Anne and
Vaudreuil are more or less national in their character on account of the traffic they would carry. A very important highway, certainly one of the most important in Ontario, is being constructed along the north shore of lake Ontario and down along the north shore of the river St. Lawrence to the Quebec boundary. Another is being projected from Ottawa to Montreal, and a third county-provincial highway is running midway between the river Ottawa and the river St. Lawrence, likewise leading to the Quebec boundary. Those three highways converge towards Ste. Anne and Vaudreuil where those bridges are projected. Montreal being the commercial metropolis of this country, those bridges will carry a very large tourist traffic coming from Ottawa, Toronto and points west, and on that Account, those bridges should be considered as more or less national in their character. The minister argues that this is a matter for the provinces to finance; he has pointed out that the province of Ontario should contribute something towards the building of those bridges; but I do not think that that province should be expected to assume any financial obligation as regards a bridge of that kind as it would be wholly within the limits of another province. In view of the nalture of the traffic which those bridges would be expected to bear, the Federal Government should assist in some degree towards the construction of those bridges. The -communities in thait portion of Ontario feel that those bridges will be a great benefit to this country in diverting through Onltario tourist traffic which now goes through the State of New York.

Is it necessary to spend this $3,000 for repairs if we build the new 1 ridge at Banff.
Mr. ,1. D. REID: Yes, because it will be some time before the new bridge is ready.
Has there been a report that if these repairs were made the present bridge would do for this year?
These repairs are required so that the old bridge can be used till the new. one is ready.

I never heard of a town being conducted by the Dominion Govern-

ment. It has come out incidentally that the town of Banff is conducted entirely under the supervision and control of the Department of the Interior. The people there must have schools and the usual institutions of a town. How is the money provided?

The hon. member would find that information in the annual report of the Parks Branch, which is laid on the Table nvery year. Banff is not a new town. It has been in existence for twenty-five or thirty years.
Will $100,000 be the total cost of the bridge? Has the contract been awarded?
No. Tenders were called for last year,'and $189,000 was the lowest submitted. We thought that too high.
Will the minister be able to keep within the ..$100,000?
I cannot say until new tenders are called for.
Then it may cost $200,000 or $300,000.

I do>
not think it would be higher than the lowest tender we received before.
What is the estimate of the department's engineer?
Will this bridge be constructed on a cost plus basis?

No, by tender and contract.

This canal is the only means of approach to Hamilton f-or vessels coming up lake Ontario. As many as 1,700 automobiles have been counted crossing this bridge within a period of three hours.
What is the size of the bridge?

M:r. CANNON:	Has the work been
started?

No, we have to call for
tenders. *
The item says "Burlington channel," but the minister speaks of Burlington canal. Is this channel a natural stream or a canal constructed by the Government?
It is an artificial cut made by the Dominion Government through Burlington beach, so that vessels coming up lake Ontario can get into Hamilton.
Could not the bridge be built by the Provincial Government, and if not, why not?
It is a Dominion work entirely.
Is it going to be a toll bridge?

No, and it never has been.
Mr. CR.ERAR: What are the conditions under which assistance will be given by the Dominion Government in building a bridge entirely within a province?

St. Anne's bridge, for instance, is entirely within the province of Quebec on the main highway between Toronto and Montreal. Up to the present no Dominion Government has seen fit to aid in the construction of bridges that are entirely provincial.

I think this is an important matter. My own view is that a bridge entirely within a province should be built by that province. Otherwise, there would be a manifest injustice done in some cases, and there would be many demands upon the Federal Government for assistance. Is there any settled policy in granting assistance of this kind when requests are made to the department?

So far as the Deputy Minister of Public Works and I know, assistance has never been given by the Dominion Government in building a bridge entirely within a province. Assistance is only given in the case of -interprovineial bridges.
Mr. CRERAR *: On what basis is it given in the case of an interprovineial bridge?

That principle was
established many years ago. The bridge ftom Ottawa to Hull, for instance, is interprovincial. We also adopted the principle

when the matter was international between Canada and the United States, as for instance in connection with the town of Ed-mundston. There are other instances that I cannot recall.
One can understand why-assistance should be given to an international bridge, but that is in a different category from interprovincial bridges.

About two years ago I sent to the department a petition from the city of Lachine asking for repairs to a certain small bridge on the Lachine canal, and since that time I have been endeavouring to get some action taken in the matter. This bridge is in a very dangerous condition. It is too narrow for the traffic, and there is not .real safety to the public who pass over it. A young girl fell into the canal and was half drowned because there was such poor protection on the bridge. I am informed that further petitions have been sent to the department urging for repairs to this bridge, and I shall be glad if the minister will tell me what the department intends to do.

This is a matter that comes under the Railways and Canals Estimates, and when we are discussing those items I will have the deputy minister here and shall probably be able to give the hon. member more details than I could at this moment.
Capilano Biver, B.O.-Bridge-Contribution by Dominion Government, Provincial Government, and Municipality, each to contribute a like amount. 511,000.

Is this entirely within
the province of British Columbia?

Yes. We need this
vote because we built at this particular place a dam which necessitates a bridge. This $11,000 is the Dominion Government's share of the cost of constructing the bridge over the river to replace the one damaged in January, 1018.
Was the dam built for Dominion purposes?

The deputy minister
tells me it was built for Dominion purposes, and for that reason we are asked to contribute to the cost of building the bridge.
Mr. iCEERAR: In this case the building of the dam made the bridge necessary?

By building the dam we diverted the water of the Capilano river into the channel and this made the bridge necessary.
Dominion-roads and bridges generally, $5,000.
This is a general vote in case we require any unforeseen work done.

We shall spend the money wherever it is required.

I wish to say something in regard to the condition of a road in my county, the county of Charlevoix, Montmorency down the lower St. Lawrence. Last year a Bill was introduced by the Federal Government giving a certain amount of money to the different provinces for the building of public highways of an interprovincial character. The circumstances in connection with the county I have the honour to represent are somewhat peculiar. As far as St. Joachim, about thirty miles below Quebec, there is a good provincial highway; but for years past communication between that place and Baie St. Paul in the county of Charlevoix and other places further down has always been by way of a highway through the bush, which has been maintained by the different parishes in that district. I am of the opinion that a highway of this kind falls within the category of the public highways which the Government purposes to build between the different provinces. Between St. Joachim and Baie St. Paul there is absolutely no proper communication by land except by way of the Quebec and Saguenay railway, and if people wanted to travel by motor or any other vehicle owing to some accident to the railway or in the winter they would have to use the old highway, which is in good condition sometimes but which is not by any means satisfactory. Now that the Government is contemplating spending the moneys voted for public highways between the provinces, I submit'that it would be only reasonable that a certain sum should be devoted to this part of the country. I am told that the Provincial Government has submitted to the Federal Government a plan of a certain proposed highway, from St. Joachim to St. Simeon, and perhaps the Government can say if there is going to be this year any appropriation in connection with this work.

This $5,000 is for the
purpose of repairing a number of bridges in the different provinces. There are some in Nova Scotia, Quebec and Ontario. With reference to the question of public highways, there was a vote of $20,000,000 passed for this work in the different provinces. The provincial governments make plans of the highways they want and submit them to the Dominion Government. We consider them with our officials and if we are satisfied with them we agree to the 40 per cent. But the Dominion Government does not dictate as 'to where the money is to be spent, once having agreed to the plan. As to a special vote for the particular locality mentioned by the hon. member, it strikes me that this is almost entirely a provincial matter. At any rate, the Dominion Government would not consider any expenditure unless the Provincial Government were prepared to subscribe, and it is for them to submit plans to us.

Under this item I wish to bring to the attention of the minister a certain district in the county of Timiskaming where the Dominion Government built a dam on the Quinze lake for the conservation of the Ottawa river waters. I understand that the township disclaim the responsibility for maintaining this work, and certain residents in the township of (Latchu-lippe, in the county of Timiskaming, are suing the county for damages to their property by reasons of a flood. There seems to be a question of jurisdiction as to who is responsible. They have asked me to take the matter up with the Government and I have communicated with the Public Works Department. As there has been a suit against the county of Timiskaming I wish ithe minister would be good enough to take 'the matter into fails consideration At as early a date as possible and 'tell the people 'there whether he is going to maintain the road, which is in the nature oif a dam holding hack (the Water in Quinze lake, or whether it will be a matter foT the province and 'the county to- look after.

The department are now looking into it. Where there is any douibt as to whether the department is responsible, we must 'take the advilce of the Department of Justice. The deputy minister tells me the matter is under investigation and as soon as possible we iwill get the hon. gentleman a report in regard to the position the department will have to take.
North Timiskaming'-to complete erection of bridge superstructure and repairs to substructure, Quebec Government to contribute, $15,000.

lit is ihiterprovineial.

Yes, in every case where it is an interprovincial bridge 'the Dominion Government assists it to a certain extent. Agreements are made as to the amount Ithe Government should contribute. In 'thils ease we are contributing $15,000.

I do not want to oppose the principle otf aiding interprovincial bridges hut I would not like the statement that was made by the minister to remain junchallenged; that i't is the policy (of the Dominion Government to aid bridges of an interprovincial character. , Mr. BELAND: Thits is an exception to the rule. The Government of Quebec is 'the only provincial government that is rioheT than the Dominion.
Ottawa-Hull, new bridge, to replace present union bridge over Ottawa River below Chau-diere, $34,000.
Is that bridge finished?
Yes.

I want to refer to the bridge at Grand Etang in the county of Inverness. An application was made some years ago to get a new harbour opened up there by cutting out a channel in the beach. The work was completed in 1911 and a channel widened, taking in the basin from the entrance to the present bridge, so as to accommodate the fishermen. The fishing industry has grown to be a very large and important industry in that locality, and there is no room to accommodate the in-

creasing number of boats. Would it not be possible for the minister to have the present 'bridge moved up to the narrows? He has to construct a new bridge there in a short time. If he would have the bridge moved up to the channel and dredge the basin above the present landing, it would afford much needed accommodation to the fishermen. Under the present conditions it is impossible for the fishermen to get anchorage for their boats, and the further development 'of the industry is paralysed *as a result. There are always a number of boats awaiting accommodation at this point. Two large fishing firms are established there now and others will follow when we get anchorage space for boats. The dredge is operating at Margaree; it will be through in a couple of months, and Grand Etang is only nine miles from Margaree. If the minister would consider this it would be a solution of the matter. He has to build a bridge there soon and if he would undertake the removal of the bridge up to the narrows it would not cost very much, and it would give ample room for the large number of boats there. If he would have this work provided for in the Supplementary Estimates and build the bridge, the dredge could be taken down there when the work is completed at Margaree.

I have had a report on that made lately at the pressing request of the hon. member (Dr. Chisholm), and I find that the dredging and the building of a bridge would cost $50,000 or $60,000. We are considering the items in connection with Supplementary Estimates, as promised the hon. member. I do not know whether the report is such that we may have to let the work stand or whether we may have to do it. However, as far as the dredging is concerned, that may be done, but we will look into it and see what can be done.

It would really cost that much to dredge the whole space between the present bridge and the narrows, but if a channel were cut through so as to enable boats to go up above the present bridge, after the bridge is removed, it would not cost more than $5,000 or $6,000 to do the dredging, and the completion of the dredging could be done next season. The work is most urgent if fihe Government desire to assist the fishermen. I have discussed this matter with the department every session since 1912 and put the facte in their possession and convinced them of the great urgency for this improvement.

I would like the minister to call the attention of the superintendent of highways in his department to the matter which I am about to mention. The Dominion Government have given the provinces the means of constructing highways. The Dominion Government aid provincial bridges. We have such a bridge over the Restigouche river at Meta-pedia. Having that bridge we must get to it from the highway. The Dominion Government is interested in seeing that the approaches to interprovincial bridges are in such a condition that they can be used. In the county of Bonaventure for a distance of thirty -miles you approach this interprovincial bridge over what is the main highway between New Brunswick and Quebec. The road, in that 30 miles, traverses an unorganized territory. During the last Parliament Mr. Boulay secured from the Dominion Government $10,000 to begin the work of improving that 30 miles of road leading to the interprovincial bridge. The work has been left uncompleted. I understand that it now rests with the provincial government to decide what highways are to be built in a province. As this work has been begun by the Dominion and as it leads to an interprovincial bridge constructed by the Dominion-the old intercolonial railway bridge-as it is the main highway between New Brunswick and Quebec-because you cannot reach New Brunswick by road, you cannot go from New Brunswick to Quebec, or vice versa, excepting through the Metapedia valley-and as this thirty miles of road remains uncompleted, I would ask the minister to get the Commissioner of Highways to give consideration to this question so that authority may be given to the Quebec Government to build this last thirty miles of road when we would have an uninterrupted highway between Quebec and New Brunswick over this interprovincial bridge. At the present time this bridge which would be of immense value as a means of communication between the two provinces is not used to any extent because the thirty miles referred to are unfinished. The work was commenced by the Dominion but has been abandoned. The provincial authorities have done nothing, and there the matter rests. In view of the work being of a Dominion character, the Commissioner of Highways should take the matter up and see if he cannot get the province to complete the unfinished thirty miles. Then this highway bridge could be opened up and connection established between the two provinces.

In the Restigouche

Mr. SINiGLAIR (Antigonieh and Guys-borough): There is one very urgent case, Port Hilford, on the southern coast of the province of Nova IS-cotia. of the province; but dredging has been neglected at Port Hilford to such an extent that the owners of the steamer say that it is now impossible for them to make the call owing to the fact that the mud and sand have accumulated so much at the .public wharf that there is not sufficient water there for the boat at low tide. , Mr. J. D. REID: I shall -have -a note made ,and bring the matter to the attention- of the officials of 'the department. I -shall, ho-wever, bring 'the matter to the attention of the officials of the department in order ito -see if something can be done.

In order to show my constituents that I am not neglecting their interests, I should like 'to refer for -a few (moments to important dredging that should .be done -alt Ri-verport and Lunenburg. speechtext:
I have not seen the
papers in connection with the dismissal of Mr. Scammell, hut my information is than at the time Of his dismissal he had only been on leave of absence one week. He was then alt Halifax, I believe, in training. There were charges made against Mr. Scammell, and it was on the recommendation of the assistant engineer, Mr. Du-fresne, who is not now in the employment of the department, that Mr. Scammell was dismissed. At different times when I was Acting Minister of Public Works I came in contact with Mr. Dufresne, and I have the greatest confidence in him. I always found him a thoroughly reliable and honourable man. If my information is correct, there is not a member on either side of this House who would not admit when the facts were laid before him that Mr. Scammell's dismissal was perfectly justified. If the hon. member does not know the reasons why Mr. Scammell was dismissed I shall be very glad to give them to him, so that he will have an opportunity at some future time when the Estimates are up of saying whether or not he thinks his dismissal was justifiable. I am informed that Mr. Scarn-mell has been given the reasons for his dismissal and has all the information, and if 240*
he has not already given it to Ithe hon. member he certainly should have done so before asking him to bring this matter up in the House.

If that information was in the office of the Minister of Public Works, how does my hon. friend explain the letter written by the Hon. Mr. Carvell, who admits that a great wrong was done to Mr. Scamimell?

I would take it that Mr. Carvell, who had only been in office a few days before he wrote the letter, did not know the circumstances, but knew Mr. Scammell. Afterwards, on looking over the file, he no doubt came to the conclusion that Mr. Dufresne, or whoever made the recommendation for Mr. Scammell's dismissal, was perfectly justified by the facts. Mr. Scammell was dismissed in January, 1916, or almost two years before the Hon. Mr. Carvell became Minister of Public Works. 1 have no objection whatever to letting my non. friend see the file respecting Mr. ScammelPs dismissal.

I thank my hon. friend for the opportunity of examining the file, but if there has been no investigation the file is of very little service, because on the one hand there will be the statements of the department, and on the other Mr. Scam-mell's statements, and I might feel that he had the best of the argument. Irresepective of that, I say that this man was given leave of absence to go overseas, and if he did not come up to, the requirements of a district engineer, it seems strange that that was not found out during the eighteen years he was with the department, instead of a week after his enlistment. At all events, he enlisted under a contract practically signed, sealed and delivered, that he was entitled to his pay while overseas. That was the promise made to him immediately he enlisted. My hon. friend says that within a week after he had been granted leave of absence-I did not know, that it was so. short a time

as soon as he had turned his back on the department and donned the King's uniform to carry out his part of the contract, the Minister of Public Works, through his deputy or some other official, summarily dismissed him, leaving him to fight his own way after eighteen years service to his country. If he was incompetent a week after he enlisted, he was incompetent at some period of the eighteen years he was in the public service.

Some years ago the Department of Public Works did some dredging in Little Bras d'Or in the county of Cape Breton to enable ships to get to a new mine opened up along that arm of the sea. The dredging was almost completed some years ago, but I believe it still requires a few touches to make the channel absolutely safe. No doubt the minister knows that in connection with these harbours and channels a record must be made of the depths of the water at the different entrances I understand from information received either from the Department of Marine or from some other source that this record has not yet been madie in the case of Bras d'Or harbour, which consequently is not listed. The navigators therefore have not the information as to the depth of water which is requisite for the vessels of which they have charge. I would bring to the attention of the minister the fact that the work necessary to be done there is very slight and the report should be made to the Marine Department so that the proper record might be made. The minister probably understands the situation. If you go to a captain in Halifax who has charge of a vessel and ask him to go to Bras d'Or he will ask you what the depth of the water is. The place is not listed and though, as a result of dredging, the depth is now 22 feet, he will turn up his existing record which shows 8 feet,' and it will be useless for you to tell him that the depth is really 22 feet. He will stand by the record he has. lit is therefore necessary to have a proper official' record as to the condition of the harbour. During the last eight or nine years the depth of the water has been sufficient, but the necessary record has not been made; and I would ask the minister, in conjunction with the department, to make the necessary record of that harbour. I might also remind the minister that some little dredging was done around the piers of Nova Scotia, notably at North Sydney, last fall. But the winter came on and the work has not been finished. Would it be possible during this summer to complete what was begun at North Sydney last year?
With reference to the work at Sydney

There is Sydney and there is North Sydney. Which does the minister mean?
Mr. J. D. iREID: Work will be done at both North Sydney and 'Sydney this year.

With reference to the work at Bras d'Or, I have not the details with me at the present moment, but I will have a memorandum made for the engineering staff to see if we can have the work done this year. The point raised by my hon. friend that the work done by the Government in harbours should be made public is an important one. I am informed by the deputy minister that every year a list of the various depths is sent to the Marine Department, whose duty it is to advertise any changes that have been made in the harbours and channels. I understand that they do this, and if there has been any omission in this respect I should think the Marine Department would be responsible and not the Public Works Department. I am under the impression that the Marine Department has advertised these changes, but II will bring the hon. member's point to the attention of that department to ensure that the necessary information shall' be given to the public.

I have always understood that the major part of the work was done at Bras d'Or but that there are a few lumps here and there that have not been quite cleaned out, and for that reason it was impossible for the Marine Department to make with certainty any record as to what the depth was. If they put on the record that there is a clear channel of a certain depth and width, that statement must be a positive fact; it will not do to say that part of the channel is clear but that there are lumps in the middle where a ship might ground. I understand that there were parts here and there in that very important harbour which were not quite finished and consequently the Marine Department could not make a complete record.

Of course, if there is
ne lump not cleared away the channel can only be listed at the lower depth, and therefore the hon. member is quite right when he says that the department could not make a record of the increased depth. I have had the deputy minister make a note to see just what the trouble is in connection with the place, and if there are any lumps they certainly should be cleared away at the earliest possible moment. We shall take a note of the matter and try to have the work done this year.

It was stated here
yesterday that it is a matter of great importance and urgency that coal should be freely transported. Now, there is an important coal mine on this harbour, but all shipping of the coal is done by rail. There

can be no shipments by water until there is a clear channel. I refer to the Bras d'Or Coal Company. One of our friends, Senator Currie, is largely interested in it.
Dredging-Ontario and. Quebec, $450,000.

What do
you intend doing in Quebec province under this item?
The following is a list of the places at which work will be done: Port Alfred (Quebec), Saguenay River, Three River, St. Denis (Quebec), Vaudreuil, River St. Francis.
Is this new work, or a continuation of work already begun.

Mostly work we have
begun.

Dredging
is provided in the Bay of Chaleur for the Maritime Provinces, but none is provided for Matane, 'Gascons and Rimouski in Quebec, with a shore line of 400 miles. All right.

If the
minister could send one of his dredges from New Brunswick across the bay to continue this work and to permit these boats to enter the mouth of the Bonaventure river so that these mills could be started up again and the limits operated, because they are amongst the most important in Eastern Quebec, it would be greatly in the interest of the people of that part of the country.
iMr. J. 'D. REID:	I will take it up with
the officials and see if it is possible.

Does the
minister contemplate appointing a resident engineer permanently for Bonaventure county?

No.
Mr. MARCIL (Bonaventure) I had an answer from the minister the other day that Mr. Trudeau was acting temporarily at the present time.
We cannot make any permanent appointments at present.

I am not
urging a permanent appointment but I would like to know the policy of the Government. Is it the intention to discontinue these resident engineers? In my constituency where there has been no work for the last ten years, I have often wondered why a resident engineer should be kept.
IMr. J. D. REID: The policy of the department is to cut down the number of resident engineers. We have thirty-one districts in the Dominion and the policy of the Government is to cut them down about half. But circumstances have arisen under which we have no work for them. We have a Bill on the Order Paper, if it would only go through, by which we could treat them fairly on their retirement after their very long service.

While the minister is looking into the dredging situation in Bonaventure he might ask his official to inquire into the state of affairs at New Carlisle. There is a splendid wharf at that point but it is filled up with sand. The Meig's Pulp Company of New York which has been carrying on the business of exporting pulpwood would like to use this wharf but it had to stop operations last year on account of not being able to utilize it. regrettable to think that a public wharf remains unused because of the want of a few hundred dollars being spent on dredging.
I will look into it.
The minister spoke of making some changes in the engineering staff. I understand that nothing has been done?
That is right.
The matter is open for consideration?

This is the first I knew of this -situation.' I shall take the matter up (with the officials of the department -an-d see what is necessary to- be done and what action we can take during the present year.

I .thought, while the minister w-as answering the hon. member for Bo-n-aventure i(Mr. Marcil) I heard him mention some places- where dredging, should be done -and among them the river- St. Francois. If (that -is true I would thank him for hi-s attention to -that part of -the County, (because recently demands have been made by -the people for -certain dredging to be done i-n order to accommodate schooners -and siai-l boats. Regarding the statement of the hon. member for Regina with

respect to the waters of Last Mountain Lake if I understood him correctly he said that the water of the lake was six feet deeper than it should be. I cannot concur in the hon. member's statement.
I said it was six feet deeper than it naturally was.

Well, it is not too deep at the present time. Last Mountain Lake is the only body of water in central Saskatchewan, and it provides a pleasure resort for the people in all that part of the country. While what the hon. member said, as to the water being held from off certain lands in the valley may be true, I think it is a matter that the Government should carefully consider before they take any steps to do away with the dam. Last year a move was made along the line suggested by the hon. member for Regina, and the other side of the question was put up to me as this lake is located in the constituency that I have the honour to represent. A largely signed petition was sent to me against any move towards lowering the water in Last Mountain lake and therefore I would advise the minister to thoroughly investigate the matter before he undertakes to do anything on the representations as made by the hon. member for Regina.

Will you permit me, Mr. Chairman, to speak again for just a minute. There is no intention of attempting to lower the level of Last Mountain lake and I do not wish to take the dam away. I did not say that and I want the hon. member to withdraw the statement. What I said was that I wanted a dam put in there with sluices in it so that the water could be regulated and let out what is necessary for the farmers below. That is all that is asked. I hope the hon. member will be more careful and not put into my mouth words that I did not use.	,

The hon. member is getting unduly excited. I did not state that he had said the dam should be taken away; if he wall read my remarks in Hansard tomorrow he will see that I did not. What I did say was that the minister should not pay too much attention to the representations that were made by the hon. member for Regina in his remarks. I said that the hon. member from Regina had said that some people had asked that this dam should be blown up; to this I took exception and that is all I stated.

I am very pleased to see that the farmer representative is looking
after the interests of the pleasure-seekers around Last Mountain lake instead of the farmers in the Qu'Appelle valley.
I do not wish to continue the controversy with the hon. member for Regina.
You had better not.

As far as that is concerned I think I can take care of myself, but the point is this: As I have said Last Mountain lake is a pleasure resort not only for the people in the towns and cities in that country but also for the farmers who like a day of recreation once in a whale; and if any harm has been done to the farmers in the Qu'Appelle valley others may have been recompensed to a probably larger extent and the matter should be thoroughly investigated before any change is made.

It seems to be a ques

 tion of something like dynamics that the hon. member for Regina has given us. I can quite understand that a dam would stop water until it got to a certain level, but after reaching the height of the dam would not the water go over its edge and run into the valley below?
'To a very limited extent. The water has been raised, and that is what I have been trying to impress upon the committee, to six feet above its natural level.
And then would not the water run over the dam?

It would if there was any left. But the dam is there and it carries the water into the lake. By the time it has got into the lake there is no water left to any extent in the Qu'Appelle river and there is practically none for the farmers below. I wish it to be distinctly understood that vested interests have been created by the establishment of a large number of pleasure resorts on that lake. I am not wishing those interfered with at all, and the engineering process which I recommend will not have that effect. It will not lower the level of the lake at all, the water can be retained and only such a flow released as will be required for the farmers below.
I can quite understand the hon. member's persistency.

I am Scotch.
Mr. McKENZIlE: But on account of the flow of water they have there the laws of gravitation do not seem to be the same in that part of the country as elsewhere.

It would not be biblical.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:

On section 1-Stamp taxes upon bills, notes, cheques, overdrafts, etc.

Under this clause I must refer again to the question I raised the other day about overdrafts. Take a man with a line of credit of half a million dollars and he borrows another half a million dollars; if his overdraft is uncovered for just a few days, when the hank makes its quarterly return that one million dollars would appear as his maximum overdraft and he will have to pay $40,000 tax besides the bank interest. I do not think that is in the interests of the country. Take another case of an overdraft. A lawyer, say in Montreal, is acting in expropriation proceedings for the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and the owner of the land comes to him and says, "I will sell. Give me $40,000." The lawyer goes to the hank with his papers, the bank have confidence in him, and they mark his cheque for $40,000 to close the deal. It takes some time for the voucher to go through a big concern like the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and as a result that lawyer will be taxed 2 cents per hundred dollars on the $40,000. He will lose $800, while his fee may be only $300. Under these circumstances only those who have big bank accounts and can handle large sums will be able to do business. I do not think this is the proper basis for taxing an overdraft. As I said the other day, when you give a one, two or three months' note, you get the benefit of the money,-you are at the peak load all the time; otherwise you -are not, for although -your overdraft may be for only twenty-four hours, if that appears in the bank return you will be taxed on it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Since my hon. friend raised the point it has had some consideration. To cover to some extent the extreme cases that he mentions-
They are common cases.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not know. There are not very many people, Mr. Chairman, whom the banks would allow to have overdrafts to the extent my hon. friend has mentioned.
They are not overdrafts; the money is on the way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think something like this would meet my hon. friend's objection: Overdrafts to be taken into account for the purposes of this statement shall not be deemed to be outstanding until the fourth day on which the account is overdrawn.
I am willing to accept that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is something which would remove these accidental overdrafts entirely from the operation of the Act, and would merely tax overdrafts used for credit purposes.
Could it not be extended to ten days? Four days is a very short time.

I have had it called to my attention that overdrafts are used very largely by municipalities. It is a very common thing for a village, a township, or a county council to rely on an overdraft to carry them over until such time as the next instalment of taxes come in. Under this section their overdraft will be taxed 2 cents per hundred dollars. These overdrafts often run into hundreds of thousands of dollars in the case of big cities, and even small cities frequently have $100,000 overdrafts. I do not think the section will hurt merchants to any great extent because as a rule overdrafts are very unpopular with bankers. I do not know whether the minister has had this called to his attention, but it is certainly a very important matter for municipalities.
After all, this is a very small tax. In the cases mentioned by my hon. friend from Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) it would be $8 and $200 instead of the figures he has given.
But it keeps recurring.
It is a very small tax.

I have sympathy not so much with the municipality that has to borrow money, because they can afford to pay this tax, but with such a case as that presented by the hon. member for Three Rivers

(Mr. Bureau), where a business man or a firm borrows $40,000 or $50,000 in the way of overdraft, for in such a case it becomes a serious tax if repeated several times in a year. With the high rates of interest, with banks charging 7 per cent and liable to charge more, and with the tax on one's overdraft which may occur several times during the year, the item is a serious one.

I would
like to support the contention of the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau). I have a case in point of a firm who are doing business as cattle buyers and meat packers, whose capital is somewhat limited, but who are serving a very useful purpose in the community in which they do business. These people inform me that they require to borrow from the bank very large sums of money on short-date notes, it may be five days or it may be ten days, and they are doing this throughout each month of the year, covering up in five or ten days, as the case may be, with the result that, during the who)e year's operations, they use an aggregate of a quarter of a million dollars. This tax of two cents cn each $100 is going to be a serious obstacle to their financing, and would effect a hardship on concerns carrying on such a tremendous business on such a small capital.
Does not the hon. member note that the tax on an aggregate of a quarter of a million dollars is only $50. It is one-fiftieth of one per cent.
I do not understand it as such, if the firm gives a note for $10,000 to-day, payable'in five days or ten days, and two weeks hence, another note for $15,000 and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
That has been covered. When the proposals were first-made, a great deal of opposition was taken by hon. members because, for exemple, in the wheat business, you have an accumulating account, an account which changes day by day. You may have an account for $5,000,000 to-day, evidenced by a demand note. To-morrow that account is slightly changed; the debt may then be $5,250,000, or a little under it, and so on throughout the month. That, of course, would have meant a multiple of taxation upon the same line of credit. When the first resolution was brought down, I did not appreciate that there was this large amount of duplication of demand notes which would pyramid the tax, small as it is. Therefore, in order to get away from that, I have changed that entirely in the Bill. The Bill to-day pro-

vides that, in case of these demand notes being given' by the elevator companies, there shall be no tax on those day-by-day transactions, but that the only tax that is put on a demand note is the initial payment of two cents, and that during the credit period, which is defined as a three-months' period, there is only one tax paid on the multiplying scale. That is, two cents for every $100.
Four times a year.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes. That is taken upon the maximum of the credit.
That makes the tax eight per cent per annum in addition to the interest.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
The tax is one-twelfth of one per cent.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: The minister has submitted for an illustration the wheat business, but is one not really pyramiding the charges in the wheat business? For instance, when a farmer brings; his wheat to the elevator, the elevator man gives him a cheque, on which he puts a two cent stamp. Then he puts a two cent stamp on the note that is given for the payment, the money advance the farmer requires. Supposing the wheat is sold the next day, another two cent stamp has to be put on the draft he makes on the buyer. The minister is pyramiding these charges three times.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not read the Bill. There is only a two cent stamp on the cheque. There is only a two cent stamp on the draft. It is only on the instrument carrying credit for a length of time that the multiple tax comes in. If it is a three months' bill of exchange, the matter will be quite different. But in the case the hon. member illustrates, the result would not be that. The man would put a two cent stamp on his cheque and if he sold the wheat the next day in sending out a draft he would put a two cent stamp on his draft. As he had just bought and sold in that way the chances are that the transaction would be carried out ion his own running credit. By the method proposed, so easy does it become that you could have thirty daily transactions in the course of your month involving a credit of $5,000,000, with only a tax on one transaction. The concession As even greater than that: you can have, during a course of three months, 241
ninety daily transactions with a tax only on one.

Supposing a man gives a note for $1,000, payable two months hence. He has to put on that a stamp tax of 20 cents. At the end of two months he pays $200. Would he have to put a stamp tax of 16 cents on the renewal note for $800?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Yes.
;Mr. OOPP: Supposing he makes a note . for $1,000 for a year, and at the end of the first month he pays $200. That is the same thing exactly, but he is paying taxes twelve times for renewals.
M-r. STEVENS: The holder of the note could endorse the payment on the back of the note.
If the man renews the note, it is exactly the same transaction, but in the case of renewals he pays the tax every time, although the first time he paid 20 cents.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The amendment that I suggest to get over the overdraft difficulty is this: I move to amend clause 1 by inserting after the word "bank" at the end of the sixteenth line on page three of the Bill, the following words:	*
An overdraft to be taken into account for the purposes of the statement and the value of the stamps to be affixed, shall not be deemed to be outstanding until the fourth day on which the account is overdrawn.

Perhaps the minister will explain the purpose of that amendment. [DOT]
Sir HENRY DRAYTONi: The idea is to prevent a tax on an accidental overdraft, something which has happened resulting from delayed payment of a cheque, something which was not at all anticipated by the parties, something which really does not evidence a specific credit -transaction. There is no tax whatever on this accidental overdraft of less than four days.

This seems to be rather a stiff tax. As I understand- it the tax is based on the maximum borrowing in each quarter of the year. For instance, if a concern has borrowed $5,000,000 to carry on its business it pays a tax of two cents on each $100 for the first three months. If it borrows $6,000,000 in the next three months, another two cents per hundred dollars is added and so on through each quarter of the year. That is a very considerable tax on credits, and it works out rather unfairly in this respect: A



company, for instance, that is working largely on its own capital, through having a large amount of paid-up capital, will be taxed comparatively a small amount, and will also escape in large measure the business profit tax, whereas a concern with a limited capital, but whose credit standing is good, will pay a relatively heavy tax under this proposal and also a heavy tax under the business profits taxation.
In the case of an overdraft at the bank of $50,000 or $100,000 which the bank allows to stand for three or six months or a year, is the tax repeated in each quarter?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The tax on overdrafts is a monthly tax.
Mr. 'LALOR: That is a heavy tax.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The original
proposals have been changed because we thought they were too onerous. I feel sure that when the hon. member (Mr. .Crerar) realizes the reduction we have made from the original proposals he will be satisfied with this tax. The reductions being made in connection with the grain business are in the ratio of 30 to 1, that is to say, where the original proposal proposed a tax of $30 under the present proposal the tax is $1. Where a man was enjoying a very large bank credit, say of $5,000,000 for eight months, the whole tax would only be $2,000 under the present proposals.
iMr. 'CRERAR: I do not quite understand that from my reading of the clause. If a concern in the first quarter of the year has a maximum borrowing of $6,000,000, the tax for that quarter of the year would be $1,200, and the same continues through each quarter. I would suggest that the bank should be called1 upon to make the return semi-annually instead of quarterly, which would cut the tax under these proposals in two.
It is monthly.
No, quarterly.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is quarterly so far as demand of brokerage notes are concerned, and monthly so far as overdrafts are concerned.

I would cite the case of a man who bought $100,000 of Victory Bonds because he felt it to be his duty. He has an overdraft at the bank, in consequence, off $50,000. He has paid for half the Victory Bonds, and still has this overdraft of $50,-

000. Now at the end of the year he will be called upon to pay a tax of $200 odd under this proposal. That is a pretty stiff tax. Another thing: Banks do business in this way. Instead of giving a note for three or four or 6ix months, business to-day is largely carried on by demand notes. As the money comes in from your customers, the demand notes are paid off, and as a result you are giving new demand notes from day to day or week to week. It is a pretty severe tax.
They are all severe.
This one hite the man that borrows money, not the man that has money.

It appears to me
from a reading of paragraph (13) of subsection 7 that this tax on the transfer of stock may have to be paid many times in the year, though I am not quite clear that the sale must embrace a transfer on the books of the company. For instance, there is the scrip issue. What I want to know is whether every time that scrip is bought as a speculation or a temporary investment, if it is not transferred on the books of the company, is the 2 cents collected every time the scrip changes hands? Then take mining shares. A mining share of the par value of $100 is often sold for $5 or $10. Would you put a 2 cent tax on that share because it had a par value of $100? It appears to me that this provision is not very clear. Does it constitute a sale every time scrip changes hands, or only when there is a transfer on the books of the company and the stock is registered for dividend by the proper owner?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: On every sale.
When transferred in the books of the company.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Every sale.
Most of these sales are made on the stock exchange.

Regulations
will he made at the earliest possible moment after the legislation is adopted.
