What steps have been taken towards reorganizing the Mines and Geological Survey branches?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: i'miproived. I have been greatly impressed with the possibilities1 of the department since I took the responsibility of administering it.
In what' way were the resignations "disastrous"?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: These men that have resigned have not yet been replaced?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. We are seeking to replace them. Some have been replaced, but not the technical officers.
Will the minister give us the names of the men who have resigned?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes, I have the list here. In the Mines Branch, Technical officers T. W. Hardy, F. W. Bari don, R. E. Gilmore, R. C. Ganteio, William Campion, John Blizard, and G. C. McKenzie. There are some clerical officers as well.
What are the salaries of the technical officers?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: One man resigned twice. When he resigned first his salary was $1,600; when he resigned the second time his salary wias $2,200.
If he had kept on resigning he would have got the right figure.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, he is on the wiay. The salaries of the other men were: Mr. Baridon, $1,700; Mr. Gilmore, $2,300; Mr. Ganteio, $1,900; Mr. Campion, $1,600; Mr. Blizard, $1,700; and Mr. G. 0. McKenzie, $2,400. These salaries are exdlhsive of the bonus, which would be applicable in certain cases.
What are the qualifications of these men?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Hardy was assistant engineering chemist; Mr. Baridon the same; Mr. Gilmore, research chemist; Mr. Cantelo, assistant engineering chemist; Mr. Campion, mechanical draughtsman; Mr. Blizard, technical engineer; and Mr. McKenzie, as all are aware, was the Chief of the Ore Dressing and Metallurgy Divis-
ion which conducts a considerable establishment in the southwest end of the city.

What I wanted to ascertain particularly was the qualifications of these men. In discussing this matter with the Committee on Industrial and Scientific Research the .statement was made that certain employees, or officers, in the Department of Mines were .required not only to be graduates in science of a university, but .also to have a Ph.D. post-graduate qualification and several years' field experience.
I would like to ask the .minister if that is true, and -What salaries the Department of Mines pays to such men, if any are employed and such requirements are demanded.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
The qualifications to which the hon. gentleman refers have been required not directly but in some degree, as he defines them, in the Mines Branch, not in the Geological Survey. I have read the resignations from the Mines Branch.
I will now read the resignations-with the duties and salaries at time of resignation- from the Geological Survey.
And the requirements?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
They will be evidenced _ pretty much by the duties, but II will give a further indication when I have finished reading the names: L. Reinecke, geologist, $2,700; L. D. Burling, assistant invertebrate palaeontologist, $2,800; J. R. 'Cox, topographer, $2,000; J. J. O'Neill, geologist, $2,600;
B. Rose, geologist, $2,400; A. O. Hayes, geologist, $2,400; B. R. IMacKay, geologist, $2,400; E. L. Bruce, geologist, $1,950.
The system was adopted of securing these meii, towards the end of their university course, for summer work, choosing them from the most successful students in our universities. Then, those that were most successful in the service and showed the greatest promise were encouraged to take further training, and those who took the Ph.D. work were given the preference. That was an additional qualification, though not an essential1 one, because many of them did not have that degree. Mr. Brock, who was Deputy Minister of Mines for some time, worked this method of selection by co-operation with the universities and I think obtained by it some very competent and highly qualified men. As a matter of fact, unless we have men of the highest qualifications-that is the very best in their line-in this work, the department might just about as well close its doors. 'There is no use in having even

moderately good men; we must have for this class of work the best men or we cannot have an efficient Mines Department and Geological Survey. We feel that we have there a good' many of the best men yet; and while there has been some degree of disintegration it has not proceeded to the irreparable stage. I want to point out this too:	The limitation, of the salaries
at least, is not the sole responsibility of the minister of the department nor yet of the Governor in 'Council. The fixing of these salaries, minimum and maximum, is the primary responsibility of the Civil Service .Commission. The need of men of first efficiency has been pressed upon the commission but I do not think has been taken into account to the degree that I would like to see. The commission feel that having regard to similar, or almost similar, technical officers required in other departments and their salaries, they have gone as far as they can justify.

What salary has the
Civil Service iCommission fixed for such positions?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I think I can give the new schedule. This is the re-classified scale:	Geologists $3,300 to $4,200; associate geologist, $2,580 to $3,300.

Has the minister taken into consideration the advisability of placing the Mines Branch and the Geological Survey Branch under one head, as they were formerly, in order to put an end to a lot of overlapping that is now going on?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I would not wish to give a definite opinion on the wisdom of that course until the department has been thoroughly surveyed by the new deputy minister. lI have heard of overlapping, and I have no doubt there is some; but usually when one makes a close examination the overlapping is not so serious as it at first appears. After conference with the deputy minister it may be decided to .amalgamate the two branches, but I cannot say definitely at the present time.
Mr. iSHHARD: Are the qualifications of that associate geologist at $2,580 a university degree in science a postgraduate Ph. D. course, or work akin to it, and field experience? Because if that is so li think this committee certainly ought to make a very strong recommendation to the Civil Service Commission to raise the salary. To my mind it is of vital importance that we
should have the best and most experienced scientific men to lay out the plans and to erect the lines of prospective value of the geological formations of the country, and if that university training and that field experience are going to yield only that salary, I think it is a distinct menace to the department, for you cannot hope to get qualified men at any such salary. I would strongly recommend the minister to take that into his serious consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The whole three qualifications mentioned by the lhon. gentlemen are required, with this proviso: The degree is not indispensable, but the applicant must have taken his Ph. D. work in science.
Which requires at least two years' post-graduate training.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Three years. The minister has, I may say, taken it into his serious consideration, but he would require some statutory authority to supplement his "serious consideration" to. be able to get results; the Civil .Service Commission has the final say. .

I would like to suplement
my question by .asking the minister if he does not think that the salary being fixed at such a figure, with the qualifications required and demanded, is a distinct menace and injury to the service? I certainly would not hesitate, so far as my humble opinion goes, to say it is.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I have taken the view
and expressed it with some force, that the salary, considering the indispensability of these requirements, is fixed too low.

T notice that several of the provinces have mines departments, and I am often puzzled, when a question ocmes up in my own constituency, 9 p.m. whether I should submit it to Quebec or to Ottawa. Would the minister say just exactly what the work is as between the Dominion and Provincial Governments, and whether there is any duplication of work?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot say that I could speak with anything like final authority as to whether there is not some duplication. I do not think there is serious duplication. The mines departments of the provinces exist where the provinces themselves have jurisdiction over and, indeed ownership, in the mines. 'Consequently they are not of a scientific character primarily but of a proprietorial character,

just as the Mines Branch of.the Department of the Interior administers proprietorially the mines owned by the 'Crown in the right of Canada. To that branch of the Department of the Interior correspond the mining departments of the various provinces-'Ontario, Quebec, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and British Columbia. I have not observed that there is any overlapping. The Mines Branch is an organization for scientific purposes, first o<f all for surveying and examining the geological structure of the Dominion with a view to making known such formations as will be of 'assistance to prospectors and others in getting at the mineral wealth. 'Of the value of that, of course, there is no question. Indeed, the mining men of Canada would receive with despair and dismay any .suggestion to contract the work of the Geological Survey; and the resignations that have taken place have been the subject to the most adverse comment by mining men. There can be no question of the vital necessity of that work, and no question that it can be most economically conducted in the interests of all concerned by one central authority. You cannot have a sporadic or localized geological survey; you must have one survey for the whole Dominion if you are going to have efficiency. I think I have set out as clearly as I can the fundamental difference. The Mines Department gives the same service to mining as does the Agricultural Department to agriculture.

Would the minister
enlighten me regarding the Explosives Act? I do not remember its provisions.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I was not in charge of the department when the Act went through this House, but I know it has to do with the supervision of the manufacture, storage and transportation of explosives with a view to public safety. This is $13,000 less than last year's vote.

Does the Act cover
explosives used by the Department of Militia?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Oh no; those are entirely under the Militia department.
I thought that while being transported from one arsenal to another they might come under the provisions of the Explosives Act. What explosives does this Act particularly take care of?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
If the hon. gentleman will renew his question a little later I shall be able to answer it when Mr. Ogilvie

who is in charge of that work is present. I know that ordinary explosives come under the jurisdiction of the Act. I do not know whether T.N.T. is still manufactured. The chief object of the Act is to supervise the manufacture of explosives.

The minister no doubt is exercising supervision, but we have had an appalling frequency of explosions around Montreal-at Beloeil, Rigaud and other points. The hon. member for Chambly-Vercheres (Mr. Archambault) brought the matter up a short time ago. Is there any real supervision of manufacture?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: All explosives, both those that we are familiar with and those newly discovered, have to pass a test under Colonel Ogilvie before they can be manufactured. It was with a view to getting uniform administration throughout the country that the Explosives Act was enacted in 1914. It was not proclaimed owing to war just coming on. Since that time and before the Act was proclaimed, all the provinces were consulted, and it was the desire of all the provinces that this should be worked in co-operation with their laws, and at the same time that a federal supervision should be exercised and no explosive manufactured except under regulations laid down by Order in Council and promulgated with very complete directions. Therefore, the whole matter is being worked in co-operation with the provinces, but under a general supervision exercised by the federal department under this particular Act.

A few moments ago the minister made reference to resignations that have occurred in this department during recent months. Are these resignations the result of dissatisfaction in consequence of the work done by the re-classification experts? I have been led to understand, through newspaper reports and other information, that there has been considerable dissatisfaction all through the service as a result of the re-classification done by the experts brought in by the Government from the United States to re-classify the work and salaries of the Civil Service. The facts stated by the minister seem to confirm the impression that obtains, at least on this side of the House, that it was a decided mistake on the part of the Government to bring in these experts from foreign countries to overhaul and reclassify the Civil Service of Canada. It is certainly generally understood, \vhether it be true or not, that many of these resignations are the result of
/

dissatisfaction and are made as a protest against the treatment received at the hands of the experts that came to do the re-clasei-fication work.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I stated that this situation was to some extent the result of a feeling that re-classification did not afford sufficiently high salaries; but associated with that thought must be this, that at the present time owing to the high price of minerals, a great deal of mineral development is going on in the world and an exceptionally strong demand is being made for geologists, who are consequently able to command very high salaries in the outside world. It may be very seriously disputed that we should take cognizance of a possibly temporary situation of that kind and seek to compete, say for the time being, with these outside demands. I do not know that the committee is particularly responsible. The Civil Service Commission have thoroughly reviewed its work; the matter has gone to appeal; it has been heard by the board of hearing, and I do not think the experts to whom the hon. gentleman refers are on the board of hearing. The work has all been reviewed by the Civil Service Commission, and, therefore, the Civil Service Commission are responsible. I believe they are acting as they think right, and I believe they could make out a strong case if they had to argue the matter before the hon. gentleman or any one else. Comment has been made that consideration has not been given to the fact that only top men are of use in this work. The commission feel that consideration has been given to that point. I do not think I can say anything further except that there has also been comment that their energies were not leading to sufficient results owing to the lack of strong enough control and organization in the department, just of late years. We expect, however, that that will be remedied before any great length of time, and it is being remedied.

"Where these specialists
have decided upon a certain classification and salary, the Civil Service Commission are influenced by this decision, and they take that as their guide entirely in determining on a matter of this kind. It should be possible for the Dominion Government to retain the services of good men and to pay as good salaries as those paid by individuals or corporations or companies in the mining business. No doubt the department, in order to do good work along the lines laid down, must obtain and retain the
best service possible, and in order to do that, they must pay the best salaries going for the time being. Unless that course is followed, I am afraid a success will not be made of this branch of the service.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid if the department did that and paid the best sal- , aries that can be had just at the present time, the Civil Service list would reach such a total that the hon. gentleman would take a fit.

If that be the judgment of the Minister of the Interior, Mines, Oil and Gas, he is badly mistaken, because I believe in obtaining the best service and paying the best possible price for that service. It is impossible for the Dominion Government or any corporation to obtain that class of superior service unless they rise equal to the occasion. They must in every instance pay the best price if they expect to retain the services of good men. The experience that the minister has referred to tonight of his department in regard to this matter shows clearly the need for the department to pursue a course of that kind.
I do not mean to say that the department should be held up on oocasion, but they certainly should strain the salary line to the limit even under the present salary conditions, in order to retain the services of men they have tried and proven, men they know to have the experience the department requires.

What development has been made in regard to the treatment of coal in the West by the Lignite Committee?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I set out in pretty full detail in the House about a week ago what the Lignite Committee did, but this is a time when that might well be repeated to this committee. The Lignite 'Committee consists of Mr. Ross, an engineer of Montreal, as chairman, Mr. Leslie Thompson, secretary ; a representative of Saskatchewan, Mr. Shepherd; and a representative of Manitoba, Mr. Learning. Their duty has been to seek to discover some method of briquetting lignite coal and of producing the briquettes at such a basis of cost as will make the product commercially feasible. They have succeeded to the extent of proving that the carbonization of this coal is possible, and they have also dis-

covered and established the binders that must be used, some three in number, which will all be used together. They further believe that they have finally established that the amount of binder required will be twice what is required for the briquetting of -German coal, but even that extra cost is not considered a too serious impediment. The hinder I Ithink is all procurable in Canada. I mentioned to the House on a former occasion the three binders that they have discovered; I cannot recall them just at Ithe moment. As to the carbonization, however, (which, being interpreted, means the oozing out of the volatile matter, the waiter and other incombustible matter from the coal) they have discovered a method of doing that successfully. The binder ties the padticles together after carbonization. That constitutes the briquetting of coal.
They have now called for tenders for the construction of a plant in the neighbourhood of Estevan for carrying on this work as a commercial proposition. On the basis of this year's costs, instead of the costs in 1917 when the arrangement with Ithe two provinces was made, it is going to require $600,000 instead of $400,000. We subscribed $200,000 of that $400,000, and the provinces $100,000 each. I have submitted to the two provinces the desirability of their subscribing $50,000 each of the balance, and have received an answer from Saskatchewan in the affirmative, but have no answer as yet from Manitoba. Conditional on their subscribing their share, I purpose to ask Parliament in the Supplementary Estimates for the share of the Dominion.

What salary is paid to
Messrs. Ross, Thompson, Shepherd and Learning?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: No salary.
Is Professor Macallum oT* the board?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
He is in another post
altogether, under the Department of Trade and Commerce. He is not connected with the Lignite Board.
How -much does he -draw?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I believe it is $10,000, but I should not like to have to answer for any more departments than I have.

Do you know what he
does?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I have had considerable to do with him, and what I had to do with him was always very satisfactory.
What is his position?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: He is at the head of the Bureau of Scientific Research.

Is that a a branch of
this business?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No.
Who started this business?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Speaking from memory only, I believe it was on the .suggestion or recommendation of that bureau.

Is the country paying
Professor Macallum $10,600 a year foT suggestions? What does he do- to earn his money?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I cannot answer for
Professor Macallum because he is not in this department, but I should say that if he makes good enough suggestions he would be cheap at the money.

What is being done at
the peat field at Alfred in the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I should refer to that
in this very connedtion. I do not know that I can do better than read to the committee a report which I have just received, and which I have not yet had time to run over, from Mr. Haanel, who. is in charge of the Peat Fuel 'Committee. This committee was appointed by the Federal Government and the province of Ontario on a 50-50 basis to investigate the commercial possibilities of the harvesting and sale of peat in the province. I can say, briefly: The committee has made very substantial progress. They had first to get the right to the peat bog where they proposed to conduct the experiments and do the work. The peat bog that they desired had been alienated and they secured the lease of it. and have been manufacturing peat there. Last year they manufactured several thousand tons. They have tested it, and it has proven a success. This year they expect to manufacture 14,000 tons. They have no difficulty in disposing of it at the price they have been asking, of $3.50 a ton, which in Ithe opinion of Mr. Haanel represents a profit of about 50 cents a ton. Peat at $3.50 a ton is about equal to $7-a-ton coal.
Is Ithe price $3.50 at the mine?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
F.O.B. the mine at Alfred, in the county of Prescott. The object of the committee's investigation was to de-

termine whether peat fuel could he manufactured on a commercial basis in those portions of Canada where large peat deposits exist which are now dependent on foreign sources for their supply; also to determine the type of machine which can be employed to the best advantage in the manufacture of peat fuel under the conditions obtaining in Canada; to create a market for the peat fuel, and ascertain the methods which should be employed for its distribution from the bog to the consumers. A .satisfactory solution of the problems presented in the manufacture of peat fuel will render available the large areas of peat bog in the province.
The peat fuel committee has developed two types of machines, both of which they are thoroughly confident are going to be a success for the manufacture of peat on a large scale. They also have in process, of construction a small .machine which, in their opinion, will be utilized in localities for the manufacture of peat, not for sale in any. extended area, but merely locally. That was the chief object of their work. Owing to the advance in costs the report says that it may be found necessary to add slightly to the price at which they are selling the peat-which, as I stated has been $3.50 a ton-in order that there may be a fair margin of profit. They believe they will be able to establish in a very short time that the manufacture may be conducted successfully on a large scale, as they are working now only on a ten-hour basis, whereas the machinery, of course, can be worked twenty or twenty-four hours a day. They have equipped the plant for two shifts of ten hours each, and they believe they will establish before any great length of time that working on these two shifts peat may be produced on a large scale and sold on a $3.50 basis, or very slightly above, with a sufficient profit to guarantee the establishment of plants commercially. They will manufacture this year 14,000 tons, but they will not have it all produced and ready for sale within th fiscal year. That credit of $15,000, however, is the amount they believe they can safely rely on receiving from their sales.

What is the fuel
value of peat as compared, with coal?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Half as much as anthracite coal.
When was this 50-50 arrangement made with the province of Ontario?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: As nearly as I can recollect about two years ago.

There is a much earlier history of these Alfred experiments. Some years ago quite a large appropriation was made for the carrying on of experiments there. I dk) not quite remember what the outcome was, but perhaps the minister does.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: There was .quite a series of investigations carried on at the Alfred peat bog, and although they were not completely successful a lot of manual work was done, and they got far enough practically to establish that the whole problem was one of cheap machinery. There was no machinery of the type that would put the material in such shape that it could he handled at a profit, owing to the higher cost of labour in this country over Russia and Sweden, for instance, where they carry on peat operations very successfully. Consequently, when this matter came up again and it was pressed upon us that it was very desirable to utilize these thousands and thousands of acres of raw material, we determined to go into it again. At that time the Ontario Government were exceedingly anxious to carry on the work in some of their peat bogs. They asked us for our experts to survey the bogs, and the matter led to a general discussion and an arrangement whereby we engaged in a sense to pool our resources, and as it was largely a question of proper machinery to handle the peat to devise sutiable machinery, and demonstrate whether the manufacture of peat could be made commercially successful or not. With that object in view, two types of machines were built and operated last year on the Alfred peat bog. I understand that although they commenced very late in the year there were 6,000 or 7,000 tons of peat made. Since leaving the Department of Mines, I am afraid I have not kept in very close touch with the subject, but I believe that they are now going on with the work again with every hope of bing able to demonstrate that they can successfully develop it from a commercial point of view.
Are there any other districts where development is going on?.	*

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
No. There are other
points being surveyed and bogs are being tested, but it is not proposed to establish plants yet.	^

Gan the Minister of Customs (Mr. Burrell) tell us the process em-

ployed in extracting the moisture from the *peat?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: It is altogether a natural drying process.' The hope that used to be entertained by people who spent a large amount of money in the peat business was that they could do it by compression. But my recollection is that there never was an instance in which it paid to use compression to extract the moisture, because the amount of fuel used for the purpose would not be justified by the results. Consequently, whatever success there may be in the business will be achieved1 by the handling of the peat in its raw state quickly and in large quantities and letting it dry naturally- v
In the open air?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Yes.
This item provides for road and structural material. Has this any reference to the building of roads into the mining country in northeastern Saskatchewan and northwestern Manitoba?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext:
What material has been
found useful for road building in the western province?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am afraid I could not now give my hon. friend such an answer as would be of very substantial use to him, but I would refer him to a report which covens in detail his own iprovince and others, published by Mr. Clark, who is head of the road making branch, and which can be procured at the Mines Department at any time. It will give full detailed information of the examinations made.

What
means has been provided for the disposal of peat that is manufactured at Alfred?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: So far we have not required to .devise apy means because the demand exceeds the supply.
Where would a purchaser apply?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The purchaser applies to the plant. Fourteen thousand tons is anticipated for the looming year. In this connection it is felt that one marked feature of the success of the work has been the fact . that the engineer, Mr. Moore, has devised an altogether new type of machine. I said that there were two types in use successfully,. one, the Swedish type similar to that which was used .previously, and the other, the type devised by Mr. Moore. The type devised by Mr. Moore is considered a marked improvement, .and some improvements are being made on it this year. These two on a double shift of ten hours produce 240 tons each a day. There is also a small machine after Mr. Moore's type which produces from 15 to 24 tons a day and is used by farmers who happen to be near peat bogs.
Is the peat spread on the ground to dry?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Is it spread by spade?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: It is spread by machine on the ground.

A portion of this vote is for investigation of ore and other economic deposits. That is an entirely proper work for the department to carry on, but it would! be interesting to know what the policy of the Government is regarding the disposal of valuable deposits of ore or .mineral that may be discovered through the explorations of the officials of the department. The fact is that to a very large degree the valuable patrimony of the Canadian people has been alienated to private hands, and I should like to know if there is any settled policy on the part of the Government to conserve to the people of Canada as far as possible the values that accrue from these discoveries.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
First of all, let me
make it clear that the Mines Department does no prospecting. The Mines Department has no special relation to the mines of minerals owned by the Dominion in the three prairie provinces; it has precisely the same relation to those mines as it has to the mines in Ontario, Quebec or New Bruns-

wick, and it does its work without discrimination throughout the whole Dominion. If there were tb be any change of policy in the connection discussed by the hon. member it would require to be by the Mines Branch of the Interior Department, which administers the mines:	owned by the
Dominion on Dominion lands. The question is really one that should come up on discussion of the Department of the Interior Estimates, but I may add just a word to what I have already said. We have moved in the direction of reserving the mineral royalty right more generally than has been done in the past. I might refer particularly to oils. In 1910 authorization was given for the issue of oil leases with absolute exemption from royalty until 1930. The right was withdrawn on my recommendation some months ago, and no leases have been issued 'since with any exemption. All leases have been issued in such a form that we can at any time impose whatever royalty we feel is just in the interests of the whole people; and that, in my humble judgment, is the best way for the Dominion itself to reserve its interest in the common deposits of wealth in the country. Furthermore, since that time, all leases that were in arrears have been as rapidly cancelled as we felt was justifiable having regard to all the circumstances, so that these areas would come within the non-exempt areas and be subject to royalty .in connection with future locations. Speaking on the basis of information I have at the moment, I do not think there is any exemption from royalty now; there was exemption in regard to oil but it has been taken away. So, that the Dominion is in a position, over its minerals anyway and so far as I know over all natural deposits, to exact whatever royalty the representatives of the people think to be fair and right.
Is there any standardization of royalty, or does it vary according to output?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The royalty on coal?
II am talking about oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
There has been no
royalty fixed on oil but all the leases are issued in such a form that we can impose a royalty if we so desire. We have never fixed a royalty, for the very obvious reason that there has not been any oil discovered.

Not in the Mackenzie
basin?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No, there has been no oil discovered in commercial quantities in Western 'Canada. On the other hand, by long standing custom, the Dominion pays a bounty on oil production at the present time. I doubt if, without that, there would be very much oil production in Ontario. That does not affect the West because the oil produced there does not come within the standard, but there would be very little production in Ontario if it "were not for the bounty. If oil is discovered in commercial quantities in Western Canada the question of imposing a royalty would be up for immediate consideration and I would say that there would be a very good argument for imposing it.

Do the leases contain a provision reserving the right to impose royalty?
iMr. MEIGHEN:	I am not certain that
they contain it, but I know a lot of the old leases contain a clause that they are not subject to royalty.

Why should there not be a distinct stipulation within the terms of the lease with regard to royalty? I think it very desirable that the man .who takes a lease shall have it before him that at the proper moment the department may impose a royalty. I think the statement of policy by the hon. gentleman in that regard is quite correct.

I think the policy announced by the minister is a sound one. The necessary steps should be taken by the department and the Government to prevent the holding of valuable mineral deposits of this kind out of use for purely speculative purposes. It is a fact that in Western Canada at any rate, where we have very valuable coal deposits, large areas have been alienated to private individuals having in view the speculative values that may arise out of the holding of them until a demand develops for the commodity. That policy is not a sound one and it only works hardship in the long run to our own people.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I thoroughly agree with hon. members, but that question was fully covered by the Act of 1914 prohibiting the issue of any grant of natural resources other, of course, than surface lands, and as a consequence all mining grants are made by way of lease and are subject to a development clause. The parties must de-

velop the property or they cannot hold the lease.
That does not apply to leases issued prior to 1914?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: No. Those issued prior to 1914 are not under our jurisdiction. These are civil properties owned by individuals or companies, and we could not impose any requirement on them. If it is to be imposed at all it would be imposed by the different provinces. They would have jurisdiction to do that if they saw fit but we cannot do so. Wherever we have juridiction we do put in that clause. We do not allow any one to hold a mine for speculative purposes; he must develop it.

The minister might suggest to the Minister of Finance that there is a possible way of getting revenue by imposing a tax on the valuation of these mines that are held out of use. I know of no method that would more rapidly bring them into use.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That may be so, but I think there would be no method that would more rapidly bring us into contact with every local government in Canada.

Has the minister
any information as to the proportion of land that was alienated to the pirates prior to 1914 and how much remains in the possession of the Crown at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I know very little
about pirates; I cannot tell what amount they got. With respect to coal I think that vats areas are still held by the Crown. I speak with some hesitation. A great deal, of course, has been .alienated, but a great deal of development has taken place as a result of that alienation. It is not alienated out of Canada. It is still here and will be developed if it pays to develop it. As respects oil, the great bulk of the areas is held by the Dominion. The Dominion lands have been pretty well scoured for oil and we have now under consideration the question of opening our forest reserves under restrictions to oil prospecting. I cannot say whether it is likely to be done or not but a very strong argument can be made in favour of doing it.

Might I suggest that if these leases do not contain a provision with regard to the imposition of royalty it might be worth while to consider whether it should not be put in. The conditions of the lease should be well known and they should be set out in,the lease itself. These leases
[Mr. Meighen.l
are taken to capitalists and investors; they become the basis on which transactions take place; they pass into the hands of strangers who do not understand our laws, and it is desirable that every lease should contain a clear statement to the effect that it is subject to a royalty.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: When the bon. gentleman spoke about that I made a note of his point and I .fully agree that there should be such a reservation.
Does the minister know of any real prospects of oil, or has he ever known any "pirates" that have made fortunes out of the coal business in Western Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
As regards coal, I do
not think there has heen any substantial money made in Western Canada. Indeed, there has been more lost than made. As regards prospecting for oil, the country has received in oil rents and permits more money, I fancy, than any person ever got for oil, to say nothing of the cost of developing i't. It is an entire fallacy-all this imagining and prating through the country about alienating our resources to wealthy men such as oil land and coal in Western Canada. The country has got more out of the oil possibilities of Western Canada than anybody else. The country is at the winning end of the ticket every time. I do not know whether the prospects (can be said to be good or bad', but certainly I do know that responsible people and very strong companies are at the expenditure of a great deal of money prospecting the West, following the geological lines indicated by the geological branch, and I think they will yet discover oil in commercial quantities. I believe they are fully confident that they will before long discover a very profitable source of oil production.

I know they have certainly not discovered any oil in commercial quantities and they are spending money by the millions trying to discover it. I would like to ask the minister one more question: That ife. how much money the people of the country ever got out of mines of any kind-gold, silver, platinum, coal, oil, or any kind-as long as those minerals Nv in the rock where nature had placed them?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: That question answers itself; nobody gets anything out of any mineral as long as it stays in the ground.

I am tired of hearing so much harping about the natural resources

of the country and not allowing "speculators" to have anything to do with these minerals-that they should be kept there for the people-when so far as I know they have been closely buried, and I never heard of any prehistoric man making any money out of them. I do not know why the people of the present day should be supposed to put their money into these mines and develop them without having the opportunity of making something out of it. All that sort of talk is so silly I cannot help protesting against it.	[DOT]

I must protest against the statements of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nesbitt) because the greatest alienation that ever took place on this continent was the alienation of the anthracite coal fields of Pennsylvania, and all America to-day is suffering from it. A combination of coal mine owners and railroads got those coal fields absolutely in their hands, and they have monopolized them and made enormous fortunes. We need to use that coal to-day and have to pay an enormous price for it, whereas if the State had exercised the same discretion and foresight that has been exercised in some cases in Canada the people would have had the benefit of it. Both the provinces of Quebec and Ontario are enjoying large incomes now because they designed a lease with respect to pulp and timber lands whereby they get a continuous revenue out of those lands, and the condition governing the working of Crown grants of timber is such that they can be renewed every year somewhat on the line that the ex-Minister of Finance referred to.
How much revenue does Ontario get from its water-power?

It gets a cheap power for all the people of the province, including the farmers. My hon. friend does not want to see them get it; he wishes to put a monopolist operation in between. Now it is possible that these great resources have to be leased-and I have no objection to that being done-and to have such conditions imposed in the lease that the lease could be revised every year and the royalty or the dues increased, and the control of the price at which the product is sold provided for. I am glad this discussion has taken place to-night; it is in the right direction.

I would ask the hon. member before he ceases-
Mr. MACLEAN (York); I have a right to
cease.

-supposing the coal had lain in the ground in Pennsylvania all this time and that no private individuals had put their money in the mines and developed them, what good would they have been to the people of Pennsylvania or Canada?

The condition might have been much better than it is today. The doctrine we hear in some quarters is that the people cannot do anything for themselves, that they cannot develop water-power or develop anything. We have developed water power in Ontario that is to the benefit of the people. That water-power has not ibeen alienated but a big revenue is derived from it, apd the province has a great industial development under way based on it. So that this policy is not indiscreet, and the capitalists are not the only ones who can effect improvements for the public. 'Sometimes a State can do it and do it advantageously. I do not agree with the doctrine that has been stated here to-night that the only ones that can save the nation are the capitalists. Perhaps the people sometimes can save themselves if they have the chance.
The minister seems to have no confidence in the possibility of the production of oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I stated the very opposite.
You have confidence, but there is no production of oil.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We have oil in commercial quantities in Western Canada.

The reason I asked the minister if he thought we had oil is this: A short time ago a charter was granted *to a certain company to build a railway in the Northwest. When the application for the charter came before the Railway Committee the lawyer representing the company said he thought there would be some oil found in the district to be traversed by the line but he was not sure.
Mr. ARMiSTRONG (Lambton): They are drilling in that district now.
They are in Calgary too.

But the promoters of this company are -not sure of finding oil. I was trying to ascertain from the minister why a charter should be granted to a com-

pany that did not know whether they would be successful or not in their enterprise when other charters had been refused prior to that, although we claim that we have great resources in timber, and agricultural lands, and so forth.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I am sorry I cannot answer both for the Government and for the House. As to the Bill the toon. member refers to I never heard of it myself, but I presume it is a private Bill granting a franchise to build a railway. I would expect that those who are getting the franchise anticipate developing oil in the neighbourhood of the proposed railway?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Well, I spoke in these terms: I said I believed that those prospecting for oil in the Northwest were confident that they would be successful in getting it in commercial quantities. If they are right it is quite probable that there is reasonable ground for those people seeking to build a Toad. I do not see any objection to it myself, but it is not a matter that the Mines Department has any responsibility for at all. If there is any responsibility on any department other than the House- because it is a private Bill-it would be on the Railway Department. I would have thought that people would not be putting any money into the building of a road unless they were pretty confident there would be traffic for the road and very probably oil in that district.
Is there any one in the Dominion of Canada interested in this proposed railway?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not know the first thing about it; I never heard about it till to-night.

Perhaps I might explain. The hon. member refers ter a private charter that was granted to a company for the purpose of building railways connecting Chesterfield Inlet off Hudson bay, with Great Slave lake, a distance of perhaps a thousand miles by lake, river and inlet.	.

Will the
road ever be built?

There are only a very few miles of it that are necessary. There aire 250 miles of navigation on Chesterfield inlet off Hudson bay. Then ten miles of rapids are encountered, and it will be neces-

sary to connect by means of a branch railway with the Thelon river. The Thelon river itself runs in the direction of Great Slake lake and when nearing Great Slave lake there is another branch of the river which gives connection with that lake. Then theire will be a waterway for several hundred miles farther. That would carry the line to a point about a thousand miles west of Hudson bay and over a thousand miles north of the city of Edmonton. Since that charter has been granted I had the opportunity of speaking to the vice-president of the Imperial Oil Company who told me that they are now drilling north of Great Slave lake, over a thousand miles north of Edmonton and that it took them over one year to get the drilling outfit into the place where it is now located. He seemed very much pleased with the prospects of oil in that country.
At the same time it is nothing but a prospect.

Several
oil wells are being drilled in that country. Of course, they are all prospects.

I sometimes wonder if we are not too prone to overlook the tremendous wealth and energy expended by prospectors. After devoting their lives to prospecting and spending all their wealth many of these men have died poor. It is very easy to say that every possible safeguard should be enacted in order to insure to the country every possible benefit from its natural resources. During the discussion some reference has been made to timber. But .timber is a visible thing, it is not to be compared with our undiscovered mineral resources; and if you are not going to encourage prospectors it is the duty of the Government to themselves undertake the work, otherwise we cannot expect to develop those resources. The minister has stated the safeguards provided in the shape of royalties on any discoveries being made. But if the prospects are as good as we hope they are, then I think every reasonable encouragement should be given to prospectors with a view to making these discoveries of the fullest benefit to the country as soon as possible. As has been stated, these resources are absolutely of no use to the country until discovered and developed. It is admitted that we have not yet discovered oil in districts where we suppose it is to be had in abundance. That being the case, enormous sums of money and unlimited energy must be expended in development

in order to prove -whether the oil is there. We are likely to defeat the very object we have in view if we make the restrictions too severe and so deprive of the fruits of their labour, those who by their skill, energy and money have made development possible.

I am very glad to learn
from the minister that we have had some revenue from oil leases, and I certainly hope that our policy will be so shaped in future that we will continue to get proper development and at the same time not sacrifice our natural resources. I cannot for one moment agree with my hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) who appears to have been rather asleep on this whole proposition. His policy, apparently, would be to hand over all these valuable natural resources to capital to be exploited without any regard for the rights of the people. I submit that the people have certain rights in these natural resources, because they are essentially for the benefit of the .people.
I would direct my hon. friend's attention to the development of the oil resources of the United States, where practically all the valuable oil areas have passed into the hands of one concern. With what result? To-day we are paying fifty and sixty cents a gallon for gasolene, and oil companies are paying dividends of eight hundred or nine hundred per cent. My hon. friend may consider that a desirable state of affairs for this country, but I beg to respectfully disagree with him.
The revenue the Dominion has received for the last forty years from our mines and forests will not pay for the total expense of administration and surveys. Is that a satisfactory state of affairs? We have mineral deposits that to-day could have been producing a splendid revenue if they had been administered wisely in the past. I dissent from the view that we should pass this valuable heritage over to capital to be exploited for the benefit of private interests alone. If that is the opinon of my hon. friend from North Oxford, he and I are travelling in totally different directions.

I did not say that I
would give the natural resources of the country to capital for development, not by any means. I said that I would not discourage capitalists from developing our natural resources for the ultimate benefit of the people by taxing those capitalists to death before they made anything out of their development. My hon. friend says
that in the United States the oil areas are in the hands of one company. I can name him a dozen very strong companies that are in competition with one another in the United States.
Mr. 'CRERAR: The independent companies live on the sufferance of the 'Standard Oil Company.

My hon. friend should
nolt talk about things he is ignorant of. I can tell him the reason why gasoline and coal oil are so dear. There is a shortage of production all over the world, and there is a vast increase of consumption. Under those conditions oil, like every other product, will go up in price. Ii is quite true that those who have been successful in the oil industry of the United States have made money. So also have those who have been successful in the mining indusltry in this country; hut more money has been sunk in the industry in this country than was ever made out of it; and more money has been sunk in oil propositions in the United 'Sltates, I venture to say, than was ever made out of them. You have got to give capital some encouragement. Capital is a shy bird and it is not going into propositions to lose money on, especially if some one is coming along as soon as a small success is made and say, "Oh, this belongs Ito the people; it is a natural resource; we don't care anything about you, we will confiscate your discovery." That is what I am opposed to.
So am I.

Well, you say you want to leave all these natural resources for the people. I ask:	Whalt good are they lying
dormant? You must get some one to develop them. The same thing with the western prairies-if men did not come along and grow wheat what would Ithat country be worth? Why don't you say to those men, "We will let you retain fifty cents a bushel for the wheat, and we will ttake the rest for the people?"

Mr. Chairman, ever since I have had the honour of a seat in this House I have been strong for the development of our naltural resources. While realizing the merit of the argument advanced by my hon. friend from North Oxford, I find myself more in line with the argument of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). We have no assurance, bult every indication points to our having great mineral resources. I believe the Govern-

ment should take all necessary steps to develop our mineral as well as our other natural resources in order thalt we may see how far we can be a self-contained country. Representing as I do the county of Wright, with its wonderful deposits of mica and iron, I have always felt Ithat besides those deposits there are other minerals- the geological formation indicates it. I would certainly approve of the minister devolting some of this money; towards prospecting and developing whatever mineral resources there may be in the county of Wright. I thoroughly appreciate that the member for North Oxford is right when he says that capital will not go into a losing proposition. If there is something that is a sure thing, then you will find capital without douibt. As regards the matter of obtaining money from English capitalists for any mining proposition in this 'Country, the first thing that the men in England will do is to send over their engineers and prospectors to go over the territory, study it for themselves and make a report. They do not take the reports of our. own engineers. I am speaking now of what little experience I' have had in this matter. I do not say that there are not exceptions to the rule; but as a general rule, that is the way they proceed. If their engineers report that the .proposition is a sure one, they wil invest in it. Before the war we were able to get a certain amount of capital easily into the country for purposes of investment in different natural resources, tout we cannot get it to-day. We must recognize that capital is tied up more to-day than it ever was before, and there is not the' same amount of capital available for investment in propositions such as those under consideration to-day. Whilst respectihg, as I do and have far a very long time, the hon. member for Oxford North, who looks at questions in a businesslike way, I feel that the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar) ha.s advocated the wiser course, that here is something in the w.ay of a natural resource belonging to the people of this country, a resource in its infancy, one requiring absolute development, and therefore, I must approve the position taken by the Minister of the Interior.

What is the

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
We are adopting the English and the American practice. Under the old Act, tobacco was interpreted as being 10 per cent or more of moisture, When the tobacco came in-I am speaking of the raw leaf-it was subjected to an ordinary hand test, and if it was thought to contain more than 10 per cent moisture it was put through a proper test in the dryer. If it was proved by that test to contain 12 or 14 or 16 per cent moisture an allowance was made for the ex-242
cess about 10 per cent. If it was drier than 10 per cent, say 8 per cent, he was charged 92 pounds instead of 90. This testing takes an enormous amount of time. Our officers have charge of a good many factories, and find that practically all their time has been taken up in making these tests. Each test takes about 45 minutes. There has also been great confusion in the tests because in the drying some officers, will char the tobacco, and then it does not become an accurate test. It is owing to the great amount of time that is involved in making these tests and the confusion there has been that we have thought it well to adopt the American practice, which is to estimate the tobacco as being 10 per cent of moisture. What will happen is that if an importer has more than 10 per cent of moisture he will be penalized to the extent of the excess moisture. It is counted as tobacco. The trade will adjust itself. What will happen is that the man will simply dry his tobacco up to about 10 per cent moisture.

On section 4-abatements in computation of duty on spirits for shrinkage by evaporation while maturing:

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip
speechtext: What is the reason for making this retroactive?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
lit is not retroactive. It is 1920. It was urged upon us very strongly that we should make it retroactive for two years as regards liquors now in storage. It did not seem to me desirable that we should do that, so we are bringing the section into force on April of this year. Under the old system we have made no distinction between shrinkage by evaporation of alcohol stored in metal and alcohol stored in wood. This change has come about as a result of a long series of tests and experiments covering a period of years, as a result of which we have ascertained pretty accurately the exact amount of evaporation, that takes place. Under this amendment we shall come fairly near the mark of actual evaporation. It has been shown as a result of our experiments that there was a far greater evaporation, so far as alcohol stored in wood is coiv eerned, than was allowed for, and we were really penalizing the man unduly. The request to make this retroactive for two years, it seemed to me, could not well be entertained. I have therefore changed the date proposed in the Bill of last year and am making this section operative only from the first of April this year.

.COMMONS

I understand that the
Government suffered a good deal through the action of some distillers a few years ago. They passed the liquor into their tanks at freezing temperature or just about freezing temperature, which reduced the volume of the liquor considerably, and the moment it came out and reached atmospheric temperature the liquor increased in volume five or six per cent, to their benefit. I believe that the practice is different now and that the manufacturer is compelled to pass the liquor into the vats at normal atmospheric temperature of 65 or 66 degrees. This is an important matter and considerable money can be saved to the Government by a proper regulation of it.	.

speechtext: That was true some years ago, but there was a change in the regulations which fixed the temperature at 40 degrees Fahrenheit.

There is another thing.
Former ministers have stated time and again that there was no necessity for compelling manufacturers to store their liquor for two years, and-

Oh section 5-spirits warehoused for two years before entry for consumption.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
This is the point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Currie). Under the old Act as it stood no liquor could be taken out of the distilleries for two years after its manufacture. I am not thoroughly familiar with the reasons that impelled the department to enact that provision. I think possibly it was done on the suggestion that it would make a superior brand of whiskey. But since the wave of prohibition over Canada very much less alcohol has been made, and while there has been a strong demand by pharmaceutical chemists for alcohol for manufacturing purposes, for hospitals:, etc., there has been no new alcohol available, and the price of the two-year-old spirits has of course mounted up at a furious rate. It seemed to me, after going into the whole subject, that rather than abolish the clause altogether, which might result in any number of small distilleries starting up which it would be difficult to control, it would be better, during this shortage, to allow the Governor in 
Council to fix a time for the suspension of the clause in order that new alcohol might be at the disposal of thesd' people. That alcohol can be made quickly and it would be an inducement to manufacturers to make alcohol for this particular purpose, to meet the market, if they could go into the business without the necessity of keeping the liquor for two years.

I very much approve of this clause. ' The manufacturers of alcohol in Great Britain and the United States were allowed to bring their raw alcohol here and compound it and send it out to the Canadian people when it was perhaps not a month old. The reason why the two-year provision was made previously was largely owing to the supposition that if the liquor was stored in vats or barrels the fusel-oil, which is a bad element of alcohol, would evaporate. There is a method of removing this fusel-oil which the Government, ought to compel every distiller to adopt, and that is to pass alcohol intended for human consumption through a charcoal filter. Every chemist knows that alcohol can be made in a laboratory in a few hours, and it can be rectified in the laboratory by being passed through a charcoal filter. If the distillers submitted alcohol to that process there is no reason why it should not go into consumption inside of twenty-four hours after being made. Now, to leave it to the Government to determine whether the law should be suspended or not is merely to continue a method which gives a monopoly to three or four distillers and wipes out all the small distillers throughout the country, because no one would put money into a business if it took two years before he could sell his manufacture. Apart from that the clause is all right, and I hope that next session the Government will see the wisdom of abandoning the two-year provision. Minister after minister has said that he did not see any reason for it as it was not necessary, but it has never been abolished. If the Act were amended so as to provide that alcohol should all be passed through a charcoal filter the public would be perfectly safeguarded; but to let alcohol go to the public from a distillery soon after its manufacture without being put through this process is merely to cause blindness to people, as is evidenced by those who drink foreign liquors. I think the Government should see to the purity of liquor that is sold in the country.

On section 15-license to pack or cure Canadian leaf tobacco:

What is
there new here regarding Canadian leaf tobacco?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The only new feature
about this is that we have provided control over the packer. As my hon. friend knows the cultivator is licensed with a two-dollar license fee if he is growing tobacco for sale. He is allowed to grow tobacco without a license if it is only for the people on his own farm, up to thirty pounds per person. But the packer-the man who buys from the cultivator-we have not had proper control over although we have taken power without, as I see it, proper authority under the Act. And as a matter of fact the packer can evade the tax because it is almost impossible to follow his operations. At present it is almost impossible to follow out where he sells; we have no control over him. There has been in the mind of the department, in giving this whole subject consideration, the idea that the time has come to approach the American system and what is, in effect, carried out in Ontario-that is, the grower of the leaf selling to the manufacturer and before the tobacco reaches the ultimate consumer to pay twenty cents a pound excise as is done in the United States. But a great many representations have been put before us-I think some probably by my hon. friend, and certainly from various parts of Quebec-[DOT] that the leaf as grown in Quebec has not yet attained that general standard of perfection that would enable them in selling to get that price which is paid where the better varieties are cultivated, but they hope to get to that point. In the meantime, there is no doubt about it, if we cannot get the twenty cents a pound tax on manufactured tobacco, that is the excise
tobacco, the very least we should do, and see that we do it, is to get five cents on the raw leaf, after it leaves the cultivator's hands.

Does my hon. friend
dispute Ithe Quebec license?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I am not "disputing"- my hon. friend is using the wrong word; I am quoting the words of those who have made strong representations to the department that they do not yet grow in. Quebec a sufficiently large percentage of the finer varieties of tobacco to make cigars, but that" they are working up towards that stage. They grow a very excellent tobacco now. They claim that if they were growing a larger percentage of the finer leaf they could very well place all this tobacco in the hands of the manufacturers and enable the 'Government to collect the 20 cents excise. But we find that' the 5 cents on the raw leaf is not collected in very many cases because the packers, over whom we have no control, can dispose of the raw leaf with, out our knowledge. . Therefore, for the protection of the grower as well as the Government, we say that every packer must be licensed and make a return of the tobacco he handles in order that we may have . proper control.
The finest tobacco comes from the counties of Montcalm, L'Assomp-tion, and Joliette; the best apples from the county of Rouville; and the best salmon from the county of Gaspe.

I am taking a very keen interest in this tobacco question, because as the hon. member from Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) has just pointed out, the best tobacco, grown in 'Canada comes from the district of Joliette, rvhich I have the honour to represent. speechtext: No, not at all.

speechtext:
I thought I had explained that to my hon. friend just now. We licensed the cultivator, but I do not think we had any statutory authority to license the packer. If the packer ever got rid of the tobacco it was

his business to affix the stamp, but we had no authority under the statute to control his operations at all. It is in the interests of the tobacco grower, as well as in the interests of the country generally, that the packers themselves should ibe under this degree of control by being licensed. It does not mean that they will be charged any more than 5 cents when they are disposing of their stock, but it does give us proper authority over people handling an excisable article.

The minister is absolutely right, and I cordially approve of what he has just' stated. But my point is: In order to know who are the packers is it necessary to impose a fee of $50? Would not the control be just'as effective if the fee were $5 or $10?

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue

speechtext: I withdraw my objection on that point and accept the explanation made by the minister. I notice that the packer will have to give a bond for $1,000. That is a considerable inconvenience.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is
objecting very much to that figure I do not mind cutting it in half, but we must have a bond.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I do not think that
would be advisable, for the reason that in the administration of other branches of the Inland Revenue Department this question has come up, and I believe the suggestion

mentioned by my hon. friend was tried out, but in practice it proved to be very unsatisfactory. Nowadays there are so many of these guarantee companies that it is a perfectly easy matter to get a bond of $500, especially if the applicant is a responsible party. I-f my hon. friend would, rather leave the section as it is I am perfectly willing.
Mr. DENI'S: I do not want to lose what I have already acquired.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I would rather restrict it to bonding companies.
Then I will have to accept the $500.	*	.

On section 17-wood alcohol.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext:
The latter clauses are
practically re-enactments of the old Part X, which dealt with wood alcohol, except in so far as they deal with methyl alcohol and call it "Methyl-Hydrate" and also call it "poison," because it has been found that people seeing the term "methyl-alcohol," the word "alcohol" suggesting something to drink, sometimes drink it, and it has been thought better to use the chemical term " methyl-hydrate " and have the bottle marked "poison." The newer clauses are to be found in the first part of Part X and they deal with a new subject, that is denatured alcohol or methylated spirits. I think I briefly explained, when the resolution was before the House that up to the present time the department itself had been the sole manufacturer and purveyor of industrial alcohol, or methylated spirits, and now it has been thought well, on the representations of the manufacturing interests and of scientific and industrial people who are interested in all these matters of advanced industries, that industrial alcohol should be manufactured outside of the department and they will be able to get it a good deal cheaper in that way. Therefore, although the Bill that was proposed last year, imposed an excise tax of 15 cents a gallon on alcohol used for that purpose, we have wiped out the excise duty entirely; we will permit distilleries licensed for that purpose to manufacture ethyl alcohol free of duty and then to combine it with the

wood alcohol, making methylated spirits or industrial alcohol, at the lowest expense possible. They think, and I hope it may be so, that in this way industrial alcohol can be put into the hands of the manufacturers more cheaply that it has been in the past, and I shall be only too glad if their anticipations are realized and if this gives a great impetus to various forms of enterprise. That covers the main reasons for altering Part X.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On the title:

I know the hon. gentleman who is in charge of this Bill will not be greatly interested in the question I wish to bring up, but I was going to suggest that we have reached, in our legislation in this country a stage where we should revise the statutes. I notice that this Act was amended in 1908, 1910, 1911, 1914, 1915 and 1918, and now it is being amended in 1920. My hon. friend can readily understand the predicament of a man of my profession who is called suddenly to defend or prosecute a man charged with violation of the Inland Revenue Act.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: Defend, I hope.

He looks up the Revised Statutes and he thinks he knows something about the law, but he is told it has been Tevised and re-revised and amended, and it takes a couple of days to find out where he is at. The same thing is true today of practically every chapter of the Revised Statutes, and I would suggest to the minister (Mr. Burrell) and the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Meighen) that we should revise the Statutes every ten years, depending upon bow many amendments we make. Under present conditions I think a revision of the Revised Statutes is in order and has been in order for the last year or two. I would strongly urge upon the Government the necessity of having this work commenced at a very early date. The condition at present, so far as the profession of the law is concerned and those who have to administer the tax is very unsatisfactory, because of the uncertainty.

I cannot too strongly support the view which has been expressed by my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie). In this case in which I was particularly interested I had to go through all these statutes and study every one of them and make the necessary corrections. All practising lawyers are aware of this. The revision is a matter on which there would be no opposition whatever from either side of the House,
because everybody is agreed that this work should be undertaken and the statutes brought up to date as soon as possible. I do not think anybody could possibly object.

speakerposition: Minister of Customs and Inland Revenue
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friends (Mr. McKenzie) and (Mr. Denis). It is for the reasons mentioned that in this Bill we have repealed entirely Part X in order to make the Act plainer. Although I am not a lawyer or the Minister of Justice I am in thorough sympathy with a revision being made.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Title agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and-passed.

speechtext: I would submit to-the minister that there are a good many matters on which we would like to get information, and unless the minister is in a position to give us the information I think we had better not start on these estimates at this hour. We have had no discussion of labour matters this session at all, and I think it important that some opportunity should be given to hon. members to discuss labour questions. It is now 11.20 p.m., and the House sat until nearly 3 o'clock this morning.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I would suggest that we go into the Estimates and in that way we could have a better idea of the questions that are going to be addressed to the department.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
As we have not yet taken up the Estimates of the Department of Labour, to discuss them to-night, being Friday, the unanimous consent of the House would be required. I do not feel at liberty to consent.
